WW2 small-unit doctrine, restated for Assault Squad 2

Men of War Doctrine Atlas

What good small-unit play was, from the armies' own manuals, and how a tactical AI can apply it at any game size on any mod.

9275 claims, 39 compartments, 38 game rules. Nothing here has been played in a match.

Compartments

A compartment is one echelon (the size of the force), one branch (the arm, such as infantry or tanks) and one phase (the kind of fight, such as attack or defense). Stop at the summary, or open a card for the method and then the sourced claims behind it.

battalion / artillery / attack

Artillery in the battalion attack

direct supportfront-line targetssafety marginnot for everything

Artillery strikes front-line installations, AT guns, observation posts and enemy guns, no closer than 300 yards to friendly troops. Don't expect it to do what tanks or mortars do faster, or to blast wide lanes through mines. In the game this is mostly a proxy.

GERITJPSUUKUS

How it works, with numbers

US armor text: artillery hits front-line installations, AT guns, observation posts and artillery, no closer than 300 yards to friendly troops. One battery covers about 200 by 200 yards. c-USA04-0054

Do not expect long preparations without dumped ammunition, targets tanks or mortars handle faster, or extensive lanes through minefields. c-USA04-0056

A 105-mm battalion usually directly supports the infantry regiment, with liaison at front-line battalions and forward observers near front companies. c-USI06-0086

Raid fires neutralize every hostile position in reach and box in the objective. Hide registration by spreading points over more than a day. c-USI17-0076

Reported of the Germans: battalions are detached so habitually that massed preparation is rare; multi-barreled mortars and rockets largely replace it. c-GER-0015

Soviet: divisional guns go to battalions and storm groups for direct fire, with fire lines tied into the infantry plan. In an encounter, one or two batteries move with the lead element. SU02-0222 SU02-0293

Reported of the Japanese: the artillery advances by bounds close behind the infantry, its forward observers moving with the infantry. JP01-0072

UK, reported: corps artillery usually handles counterbattery. UK09-0013

Gaps: Stock bots have no artillery fire missions (AI-11), so these are mostly proxy or engine. Numbers are wartime values, not parameters.

battalion / at / defense

Anti-tank defense

ambushflanking firehold firemass

Anti-tank weapons reach position early, hide, and ambush from the flank; they never charge or chase. With enemy armor unknown, mass under central control. Guns near the front hold up early attacks and shield the mass. A reported German screen held fire until 150 to 300 yards.

GERJPSUUKUS

How it works, with numbers

Destroyers primarily kill tanks by direct fire. Ammunition stays reserved for tanks except in emergency. c-USA-0042

They emplace and hide before tanks arrive, ambush, and don't chase. Flanking positions are best. Because they are vulnerable, bare ground demands digging in and camouflage. c-USA-0048 c-USA-0050

Mass first: fewer destroyers means a larger share massed. Armor strength unknown means central control. Enemy limited to small-scale armor means spread among forward units. c-USA-0043 c-USA-0046

Organic anti-tank guns hold up early attacks and shield the mass, added as the attack develops. On a breakthrough, massed destroyers move ahead of the tanks or to their flanks, narrowing it. c-USA-0044 c-USA-0056

Company level: each gun gets flanking fire, and platoons cover each other's dead ground along tank approaches. Two platoons stay silent until the enemy maneuvers against the one that opened. c-USA-0058 c-USA-0063

Infantry nearby protects the guns from enemy infantry, and the guns protect the infantry. c-USA-0062

Don't trust impassable terrain. Forward positions start kills sooner but risk loss to infantry and artillery. Towed guns hide better but can't maneuver once committed. c-USA-0045 c-USA-0053 c-USA-0054

Reported of the Germans: guns stand in depth, dug in, enfilading or on reverse slopes, two to three per position with light machine-gun protection. Singles may engage up to 1,000 yards; main defenses usually hold until 150 to 300 yards. c-GER-0041 c-GER-0042

Soviet: anti-tank rifles, tank hunters and anti-tank guns fight the tanks while mortars, machine guns and submachine guns separate the infantry. c-SU-0029 c-SU-0019

Soviet: anti-tank weapons never leave their anti-tank area. UK: gaps in anti-tank minefields draw armour into killing areas. c-SU-3017 c-UK-3012

Gaps: FM 18-5 in this packet has the Gun Company chapter, not the TD platoon. British anti-tank is not read yet. Soviet is from the rifle regulations, not an anti-tank manual, and in mediocre OCR.

battalion / infantry / attack

Battalion attack

narrow frontweak groundfire not menno habit

Attack where the defender's weapons work poorly and cover runs close. With covered flanks a US battalion takes 500 to 1,000 yards. When the attack stalls on strong resistance, add fire, not men. Repeating the same maneuver lets the enemy read you.

GERITJPSUUKUS

How it works, with numbers

Frontage: a US battalion at war strength with covered flanks takes 500 to 1,000 yards. c-USI12-0070

Reported of the Germans: 440 to 1,100 yards for a battalion attack. c-GER-0012

Soviet: a battalion attacks on up to 700 meters, from a start line ideally within 800 meters of the enemy front on hidden approaches. SU01-0209 SU01-0210

Choosing where: where the defender's weapons work poorly, cover runs close, or his works face your artillery observation. Avoid long, observed, fire-swept open ground without powerful support. c-USI12-0057

Strong resistance needs overwhelming fire or tanks. More men do not replace missing fire. c-USI12-0052

UK: do not feed reserves into a stalled unit only to add manpower. It costs men and does not beat the fire holding the advance. Asking too much of a unit invites counterattack and lost morale. UK04-0097 UK04-0085

Failure, Soviet account: a battalion ignored heavy combat noise, kept advancing in column and was ambushed at 400 m. SU05-0091

Reported of the Germans: tactical skill undercut by habit. The same maneuvers recur, and Allied commanders exploited that. c-GER-0001

Reported of the Japanese: infantry attacks even without enough artillery preparation, and risks failure against prepared defenses. JP01-0097

Soviet: put the main blow where ground gives observation and covered approach; mass fire on enemy flanking heavy machine guns so the infantry can move fast. c-SU-2001 c-SU-2006

Soviet: the commander keeps some machine guns, AT rifles, mortars and guns in hand; heavy weapons move by bounds inside the infantry, never pausing support. c-SU-2002 c-SU-2007

Soviet: obstacle-clearing groups go first under heavy machine gun cover; attached submachine gunners infiltrate to kill key firing points at the assault. c-SU-2005 c-SU-2004

Soviet: seek a flank; a weak gap gets the main blow at once. Form up as close behind own fire as is safe. c-SU-2008 c-SU-2009

Reported of the Japanese: patrols with light machine guns infiltrate round the flanks under a frontal holding attack. c-JP-2005

Gaps: UK, Soviet and Japanese lines rest on lighter second-pass reads. Regimental context is thin here by design.

Evidence: 470 claims, 3 held back

    FM 7-5 The Rifle Battalion, 1940, leaf 56, p. 52, para 85a-b
  28. c-USI12-0106 US / own Fortified position attack: stringent secrecy, methodical start, then rapid maneuver against isolated resistances, reaching vital areas before motorized hostile reserves arrive.
    FM 7-5 The Rifle Battalion, 1940, leaf 57, p. 53, para 87
  29. c-USI12-0153 US / own Infantry alone attacks effectively with freedom of maneuver or against improvised resistance; power drops most in frontal advance on organized positions, demanding concentrated supporting weapons.
    FM 7-5 The Rifle Battalion, 1940, leaf 24, p. 20, para 36
  30. c-USI12-0154 US / own Fire protects every movement in enemy presence not masked by cover, darkness, fog or smoke; movement raises fire power through shorter range, convergence and flanking.
    FM 7-5 The Rifle Battalion, 1940, leaf 28, p. 24, para 43
  31. c-USI12-0155 US / own Exposed areas, in attack or defense, may be left vacant under flanking or long-range fire; small detours into cleared adjacent zones are allowed for cover.
    FM 7-5 The Rifle Battalion, 1940, leaf 29, p. 25, para 46a
  32. c-USI12-0158 US / own Pause on each line only to organize fires; reach vital objectives before enemy reserves.
    FM 7-5 The Rifle Battalion, 1940, leaf 32,33, p. 28-29, para 49
  33. c-USI12-0159 US / own Secure exposed flank by locating reserves there, assigning flank security to the flank unit, or detailing troops; antitank units cover approaches favorable to tank counterattack.
    FM 7-5 The Rifle Battalion, 1940, leaf 35,36, p. 31-32, para 57a-b
  34. c-USI12-0161 US / own Battalion is normally smallest unit given boundaries, following corridor limits; assign zones only to the objective; rear echelons may use adjacent advanced zones if coordinated.
    FM 7-5 The Rifle Battalion, 1940, leaf 38,39, p. 34-35, para 63
  35. c-USI12-0162 US / own Before action commander goes far forward to observe and deploy; during it, higher commanders stay seeing leading echelons yet touch reserves and supporting weapons.
    FM 7-5 The Rifle Battalion, 1940, leaf 39,40, p. 35-36, para 66
  36. c-USI12-0165 US / own Final assembly area is last cover reachable without battle, screened from air, ground observation and small arms; night local attacks may win better departure positions.
    FM 7-5 The Rifle Battalion, 1940, leaf 45, p. 41, para 70a
  37. c-USI12-0168 US / own Expect not a continuous line but depth: strong areas on main routes, light intervals under flanking automatic fire, then counterattacks against penetrating assault elements.
    FM 7-5 The Rifle Battalion, 1940, leaf 52, p. 48, para 78a
  38. c-USI12-0171 US / own Know artillery and aviation plans for destroying wire, obstacles, mines; request gaps your plan needs or adapt maneuver; plan post-assault phases lacking massive artillery support.
    FM 7-5 The Rifle Battalion, 1940, leaf 57, p. 53, para 89
  39. USI15-0035 US / own Battalion organizes its attack in an assembly area designated by the regimental commander.
    FM 7-5 The Rifle Battalion, 1940, leaf 296, para 352
  40. USI15-0036 US / own Assembly areas should afford cover from both ground and aerial observation.
    FM 7-5 The Rifle Battalion, 1940, leaf 296, para 352
  41. USI15-0037 US / own Leading company protects the occupation of the assembly area.
    FM 7-5 The Rifle Battalion, 1940, leaf 297, para 352
  42. USI15-0038 US / own Artillery fire placed at the disposal of the battalion is chiefly directed in support of the main effort.
    FM 7-5 The Rifle Battalion, 1940, leaf 299, para 353
  43. USI15-0039 US / own The battalion’s first objective should be the initial terrain feature behind the enemy’s main resistance, advancing immediately if resistance is light.
    FM 7-5 The Rifle Battalion, 1940, leaf 300, para 3
  44. USI15-0040 US / own Place the reserve company behind the attacking echelon, advancing by bounds as directed to support the main effort when needed.
    FM 7-5 The Rifle Battalion, 1940, leaf 300, para 4
  45. USI15-0042 US / own The commander observes from an OP with the best view, moving the reserve company forward to the nearest covered position as the assault echelon closes in.
    FM 7-5 The Rifle Battalion, 1940, leaf 302, para 355
  46. USI15-0077 US / own Reserve is a fraction of a command initially controlled by the commander to influence future actions.
    FM 7-5 The Rifle Battalion, 1940, leaf 318, para Reserve.
  47. USI15-0085 US / own Weapons platoon uses two motor carriers for transporting its weapons. 2 carriers
    FM 7-5 The Rifle Battalion, 1940, leaf 322, para 5c
  48. USI15-0086 US / own The battalion commander assigns missions and coordinates actions with other units within the regiment.
    FM 7-20 Infantry Battalion, 1944, leaf 5, p. 1, para 1
  49. USI15-0087 US / own The battalion commander must be aggressive, decisive, and inspire confidence.
    FM 7-20 Infantry Battalion, 1944, leaf 9, p. 5, para 3a
  50. USI15-0088 US / own The battalion commander is responsible for the condition and operations of the battalion.
    FM 7-20 Infantry Battalion, 1944, leaf 9, p. 5, para 3b
  51. USI15-0089 US / own The battalion commander must bring the unit to a high state of combat proficiency.
    FM 7-20 Infantry Battalion, 1944, leaf 9, p. 5, para 3c
  52. USI15-0090 US / own The battalion commander makes all major decisions for the operation of the battalion.
    FM 7-20 Infantry Battalion, 1944, leaf 10, p. 6, para 4
  53. USI15-0091 US / own The battalion commander maintains liaison with supporting units through their commanders or representatives.
    FM 7-20 Infantry Battalion, 1944, leaf 10, p. 6, para 6
  54. USI15-0092 US / own The battalion commander must keep abreast of the situation and the battalion commander's plans.
    FM 7-20 Infantry Battalion, 1944, leaf 12, p. 8, para 9b
  55. USI15-0103 US / own Cannon platoons support front-line battalions, with platoon leaders reporting directly to battalion commanders and accompanying them on reconnaissance.
    FM 7-20 Infantry Battalion, 1944, leaf 20, p. 16, para 22
  56. USI15-0104 US / own Liaison officers are sent to higher, subordinate, or adjacent units to gather information and relay messages. They receive detailed instructions and situational awareness before departure.
    FM 7-20 Infantry Battalion, 1944, leaf 20, p. 16, para 23
  57. USI15-0105 US / own The communication platoon includes a message center section, wire section, and radio and visual section, each with specific roles in maintaining communication.
    FM 7-20 Infantry Battalion, 1944, leaf 37, p. 33, para 53-54
  58. USI15-0106 US / own The message center section operates the battalion message center, ensuring rapid transmission of messages. Personnel are trained to perform all duties and operate in teams.
    FM 7-20 Infantry Battalion, 1944, leaf 37, p. 33, para 54
  59. USI15-0107 US / own The wire section installs and operates switchboards, telephones, and wire lines to observation posts and adjacent battalions. They maintain communication lines during attacks and defensive situations.
    FM 7-20 Infantry Battalion, 1944, leaf 38, p. 34, para 66
  60. USI15-0108 US / own The radio and visual section installs and operates radio equipment, panel displays, and pyrotechnics at the battalion command post.
    FM 7-20 Infantry Battalion, 1944, leaf 38, p. 34, para 66
  61. USI15-0109 US / own Use multiple communication methods: wire, radio, messengers, and signals.
    FM 7-20 Infantry Battalion, 1944, leaf 39, p. 35, para 67
  62. USI15-0110 US / own Battalion command post maintains wire communication with regiment and observation post, and radio with regiment and companies.
    FM 7-20 Infantry Battalion, 1944, leaf 39, p. 35, para 67
  63. USI15-0111 US / own Use visual control team, prearranged signals, or liaison planes for direct communication with aviation.
    FM 7-20 Infantry Battalion, 1944, leaf 39, p. 35, para 67c
  64. USI15-0112 US / own Tank units integrate into infantry command net and use liaison agents for additional communication.
    FM 7-20 Infantry Battalion, 1944, leaf 40, p. 36, para 67d
  65. USI15-0113 US / own Ensure positive communication between infantry and tank units down to squad and individual tank level.
    FM 7-20 Infantry Battalion, 1944, leaf 40, p. 36, para 67d
  66. USI15-0114 US / own Ammunition and pioneer platoon handles ammunition supply, minor engineering tasks, and minefield operations.
    FM 7-20 Infantry Battalion, 1944, leaf 41, p. 37, para 60
  67. USI15-0115 US / own Ammunition bearers carry supplies by hand to company areas or directly to weapons when vehicles cannot proceed.
    FM 7-20 Infantry Battalion, 1944, leaf 41, p. 37, para 60a
  68. USI15-0116 US / own Pioneer duties include road repair, bridging, obstacle clearance, and minor demolitions to support battalion movement.
    FM 7-20 Infantry Battalion, 1944, leaf 41, p. 37, para 60b
  69. USI15-0117 US / own Platoon prepares to lay, mark, and breach minefields, and disarm various mine types.
    FM 7-20 Infantry Battalion, 1944, leaf 41, p. 37, para 60c
  70. USI15-0118 US / own Antitank platoon provides all-around defense, coordinated with battalion and regiment antimechanized means.
    FM 7-20 Infantry Battalion, 1944, leaf 42, p. 38, para 64a
  71. c-USI16-0017 US / own An advance guard attack comes promptly on a broad front, most of the reserve committed, to dislodge the enemy or seize ground covering main-body deployment.
    FM 7-20 Infantry Battalion, 1944, leaf 70, p. 66, para 99e(3)
  72. c-USI16-0065 US / own Regiment usually gives each attacking battalion a terrain objective that furnishes the enemy observation, plus zone or frontage, supporting units, departure line and time.
    FM 7-20 Infantry Battalion, 1944, leaf 100, p. 96, para 130
  73. c-USI16-0066 US / own In a meeting engagement, first attack in a decisive direction wins tremendous advantage: limit reconnaissance, decide fast, decentralize weapons, commit units piecemeal as available.
    FM 7-20 Infantry Battalion, 1944, leaf 100, p. 96, para 131a
  74. c-USI16-0067 US / own Early in a meeting engagement, speed outweighs coordinated fire power; the commander builds fire coordination gradually as action progresses.
    FM 7-20 Infantry Battalion, 1944, leaf 100, p. 96, para 131a
  75. c-USI16-0068 US / own Against discontinuous resistance use maneuver, not a powerful attack: small groups infiltrate covered approaches, unopposed elements keep advancing, outflanking detachments into withdrawal or envelopment.
    FM 7-20 Infantry Battalion, 1944, leaf 101, p. 97, para 131b
  76. c-USI16-0069 US / own An organized position demands thorough coordination and great early fire power, yet prepare as fast as thoroughness allows to deny the defender improvement time.
    FM 7-20 Infantry Battalion, 1944, leaf 101, p. 97, para 131c
  77. c-USI16-0070 US / own By day, combine fire and maneuver to close, then shock to destroy or capture; fire weakens by casualties and neutralizes by forcing cover.
    FM 7-20 Infantry Battalion, 1944, leaf 101, p. 97, para 132b
  78. c-USI16-0071 US / own Maneuver raises fire effect by shortening range and gaining flank positions for converging fire, then brings attackers near enough for grenade and bayonet assault.
    FM 7-20 Infantry Battalion, 1944, leaf 102, p. 98, para 132b
  79. c-USI16-0072 US / own Envelopment usually gives best results, but initially it is seldom possible except for a lone battalion or one on an exterior flank.
    FM 7-20 Infantry Battalion, 1944, leaf 102, p. 98, para 132c
  80. c-USI16-0073 US / own An interior battalion attacks essentially frontally, seeking a penetration that exposes new enemy flanks to flat-trajectory fire and to attacks by supports and reserves.
    FM 7-20 Infantry Battalion, 1944, leaf 102, p. 98, para 132c
  81. c-USI16-0074 US / own Since fires cannot neutralize everything at once, concentrate effort in a main attack carrying part of the echelon to objectives easing the remainder's advance.
    FM 7-20 Infantry Battalion, 1944, leaf 102, p. 98, para 132d
  82. c-USI16-0075 US / own Aim the main attack at the weakest part: where his weapons and mines work poorly, covered approaches run close, or works lie exposed to observation.
    FM 7-20 Infantry Battalion, 1944, leaf 102, p. 98, para 132d
  83. c-USI16-0076 US / own Strengthen the main attack by massing most supporting fires on targets aiding it and giving it a narrower zone than the secondary attack.
    FM 7-20 Infantry Battalion, 1944, leaf 103, p. 99, para 132e
  84. c-USI16-0077 US / own Secondary attack fixes the enemy, hides the main effort, blocks reinforcement and draws reserves prematurely; so it gets a terrain objective and advances vigorously.
    FM 7-20 Infantry Battalion, 1944, leaf 103, p. 99, para 132f
  85. c-USI16-0078 US / own Attack orders do not use or distinguish the terms main and secondary attack; the difference lives in the commander's plan.
    FM 7-20 Infantry Battalion, 1944, leaf 103, p. 99, para 132d
  86. c-USI16-0080 US / own The attack plan has a maneuver part and a supporting fires part, and must secure maximum teamwork between rifle elements and supporting weapons.
    FM 7-20 Infantry Battalion, 1944, leaf 105, p. 101, para 134
  87. c-USI16-0081 US / own Giving leading companies a deep objective directly breaks the attack into isolated, uncoordinated company fights; assign intermediate terrain as successive objectives instead.
    FM 7-20 Infantry Battalion, 1944, leaf 105, p. 101, para 135a(1)
  88. c-USI16-0084 US / own Pause short of the initial objective only when reorganization is imperative; displace support weapons promptly by echelon so fire support never lapses.
    FM 7-20 Infantry Battalion, 1944, leaf 106, p. 102, para 135a(5)
  89. c-USI16-0085 US / own A full-strength interior battalion can attack powerfully on this frontage; a secondary-attack battalion may need somewhat more. 500 yd, 1000 yd
    FM 7-20 Infantry Battalion, 1944, leaf 106, p. 102, para 135b
  90. c-USI16-0086 US / own Enemy dispositions stay hidden until forced out, so the battalion primarily attacks terrain, directing its main attack at the weakest part in its zone.
    FM 7-20 Infantry Battalion, 1944, leaf 107, p. 103, para 135b(1)
  91. c-USI16-0089 US / own Hold initial rifle strength in reserve to exploit weakness, strike the final blow on an objective, replace exhausted units, or repel counterattacks.
    FM 7-20 Infantry Battalion, 1944, leaf 108, p. 104, para 135f(1)
  92. c-USI16-0090 US / own Reserve runs from one platoon to two companies; if too small, require company commanders to get approval before committing their supports.
    FM 7-20 Infantry Battalion, 1944, leaf 108, p. 104, para 135f(2)
  93. c-USI16-0091 US / own Site the reserve to move rapidly and further the main attack; toward the outer flank when enveloping, or to meet threats to an exposed flank.
    FM 7-20 Infantry Battalion, 1944, leaf 109, p. 105, para 135f(3)
  94. c-USI16-0093 US / own Obscure situation, narrow zone or flank position: one company makes both attacks; two reserve companies follow in column or echeloned toward the open flank.
    FM 7-20 Infantry Battalion, 1944, leaf 109, p. 105, para 135g
  95. c-USI16-0094 US / own Three attacking companies are exceptional: secondary attack, very broad front, limited objectives, short advance, resistance along the front; reserve is then one or two platoons.
    FM 7-20 Infantry Battalion, 1944, leaf 109, p. 105, para 135g
  96. c-USI16-0095 US / own Close-in flank protection stays the battalion commander's duty whatever regiment does; a connecting group suffices when the neighbor is ahead or abreast.
    FM 7-20 Infantry Battalion, 1944, leaf 109, p. 105, para 135h(1)(a)
  97. c-USI16-0096 US / own Detail a flank security patrol on an exterior flank, or an interior one where a counterattack could strike without coming under the neighbor's fire.
    FM 7-20 Infantry Battalion, 1944, leaf 109, p. 105, para 135h(1)(a)
  98. c-USI16-0099 US / own A coordinated attack adds about this time for subordinates' reconnaissance and orders; allow at least one and a half hours from commander's reconnaissance to attack. 30 min
    FM 7-20 Infantry Battalion, 1944, leaf 111, p. 107, para 135i(2)(b)
  99. c-USI16-0100 US / own Fires serve the maneuver plan: most available support goes first against targets most endangering the main attack, whether in its zone or adjacent ones.
    FM 7-20 Infantry Battalion, 1944, leaf 112, p. 108, para 136
  100. c-USI16-0111 US / own Close air targets must be readily identifiable from above and controlled by phase or bomb safety lines; aviation is never attached or in direct support.
    FM 7-20 Infantry Battalion, 1944, leaf 116, p. 112, para 136h
  101. c-USI16-0115 US / own Infantry helps tanks by killing antitank weapons and tank hunters, removing mines and obstacles, seizing jump-off ground, finding defiladed routes and taking over objectives.
    FM 7-20 Infantry Battalion, 1944, leaf 117, p. 113, para 137e
  102. c-USI16-0118 US / own Carry out the plan vigorously but not blindly; back the main attack while it can succeed, and if blocked, shift it to discovered weakness.
    FM 7-20 Infantry Battalion, 1944, leaf 120, p. 116, para 141a
  103. c-USI16-0119 US / own Artillery, cannon, heavy weapons and chemical mortars win initial fire superiority; rifles open beyond this range only if other fire support is inadequate. 500 yd
    FM 7-20 Infantry Battalion, 1944, leaf 121, p. 117, para 142a(2)
  104. c-USI16-0124 US / own During the attack the commander stays mostly at observation posts or with subordinates, seldom at the command post, and shapes action through fires and reserve.
    FM 7-20 Infantry Battalion, 1944, leaf 122, p. 118, para 143
  105. c-USI16-0126 US / own Never halt a company outrunning its flanks merely for alignment; protect it by bringing reserve and supporting weapons close behind.
    FM 7-20 Infantry Battalion, 1944, leaf 127, p. 123, para 143a(2)
  106. c-USI16-0127 US / own He may shoulder forward, shifting attack weight between flanks through fires and reserve, to use better routes or avoid frontal effort against strength.
    FM 7-20 Infantry Battalion, 1944, leaf 127, p. 123, para 143a(2)
  107. c-USI16-0128 US / own Keep pressing to the final objective even if outdistancing adjacent battalions, keeping regiment informed and reporting any loss of flank contact.
    FM 7-20 Infantry Battalion, 1944, leaf 127, p. 123, para 143a(3)
  108. c-USI16-0129 US / own Unless ordered, don't divert reserve or fires to a stalled neighbor if that delays your advance; help if it speeds you or protects your flank.
    FM 7-20 Infantry Battalion, 1944, leaf 128, p. 124, para 143a(3)
  109. c-USI16-0130 US / own Reserve moves only on battalion orders except grave emergency, and stays close enough to intervene before a counterattack overwhelms the attacking echelon.
    FM 7-20 Infantry Battalion, 1944, leaf 129, p. 125, para 143c(1)
  110. c-USI16-0131 US / own Advance the reserve first behind the main attack company, later behind whichever company moves fastest, guarding it against counterattack and rear infiltration.
    FM 7-20 Infantry Battalion, 1944, leaf 129, p. 125, para 143c(1)
  111. c-USI16-0132 US / own Use the reserve to exploit success where the enemy is weakening, not to redeem failure where he resists stubbornly; envelop or flank holding resistance.
    FM 7-20 Infantry Battalion, 1944, leaf 129, p. 125, para 143c(3)
  112. c-USI16-0133 US / own Taking over from a spent unit, commit the reserve on its flank in a new direction rather than pass through and repeat the unsuccessful attack.
    FM 7-20 Infantry Battalion, 1944, leaf 129, p. 125, para 143c(3)
  113. c-USI16-0134 US / own Timing commitment of the reserve is often the commander's hardest, most important decision, and it must never be fed in piecemeal.
    FM 7-20 Infantry Battalion, 1944, leaf 129, p. 125, para 143c(4)
  114. c-USI16-0135 US / own Don't hoard the reserve at momentum's expense; commit it without hesitation once the echelon is stopped or maneuver can speed capturing a battalion objective.
    FM 7-20 Infantry Battalion, 1944, leaf 130, p. 126, para 143c(4)
  115. c-USI16-0143 US / own At the last ordered objective, reorganize quickly and issue new orders; fast reconnaissance and orders are vital to exploit the initial success.
    FM 7-20 Infantry Battalion, 1944, leaf 132, p. 128, para 146b
  116. c-USI16-0144 US / own During pauses on objectives, advanced elements keep enemy contact to learn of withdrawal early and avert surprise by counterattack.
    FM 7-20 Infantry Battalion, 1944, leaf 133, p. 129, para 146d
  117. c-USI16-0145 US / own Reorganize at the final objective on or near its reverse slope, defiladed from aimed fire by the retiring enemy.
    FM 7-20 Infantry Battalion, 1944, leaf 133, p. 129, para 147a(1)
  118. c-USI16-0147 US / own If hostile interference stops both advance and methodical reorganization, troops dig in where they are; the commander fixes the line later, adjusting during darkness.
    FM 7-20 Infantry Battalion, 1944, leaf 134, p. 130, para 147c
  119. c-USI16-0148 US / own Pursuit past the final objective needs a regimental order; direct pressure advances deployed, with brief orders, distant objectives, free company initiative, heavy weapons attached forward.
    FM 7-20 Infantry Battalion, 1944, leaf 134, p. 130, para 148a(1)-(2)
  120. c-USI16-0150 US / own An intact reserve may begin pursuit at once, a new reserve forming; commit reserves promptly to prevent the enemy making a stand.
    FM 7-20 Infantry Battalion, 1944, leaf 135, p. 131, para 148a(3)
  121. c-USI16-0151 US / own In pursuit, don't wait for artillery or cannon if heavy weapons or maneuver can avoid delay; press to the limit of endurance, even at night.
    FM 7-20 Infantry Battalion, 1944, leaf 135, p. 131, para 148a(4)-(5)
  122. c-USI16-0153 US / own A reserve battalion may exploit success or hostile weakness, protect an exposed flank, envelop holding resistance, take over from a depleted echelon, or meet counterattacks.
    FM 7-20 Infantry Battalion, 1944, leaf 136, p. 132, para 149c
  123. c-USI16-0154 US / own The reserve battalion commander reconnoiters likely areas and routes, plans for all missions, and he or a staff member stays with the regimental commander.
    FM 7-20 Infantry Battalion, 1944, leaf 137, p. 133, para 151b
  124. c-USI16-0157 US / own Night relief: relieved unit withdraws once relievers are placed, possibly leaving heavy weapons; daylight relief: it stays firing until masked and the attack has progressed.
    FM 7-20 Infantry Battalion, 1944, leaf 138, p. 134, para 154a
  125. c-USI16-0158 US / own A hostile air or artillery bombardment caught during relief can inflict heavy casualties, so relief demands secrecy and proper dispersion of both battalions.
    FM 7-20 Infantry Battalion, 1944, leaf 138,139, p. 134-135, para 154c
  126. c-USI17-0068 US / own A raid attacks then withdraws instantly; withdrawal is the hardest and costliest part, and both exposed flanks make flank security vital.
    FM 7-20 Infantry Battalion, 1944, leaf 183, p. 179, para 195b
  127. c-USI17-0072 US / own Keep raiders to the minimum able to succeed; surprise, control and speed worsen with size; a whole battalion raids only with fire support.
    FM 7-20 Infantry Battalion, 1944, leaf 185, p. 181, para 197-198
  128. c-USI17-0073 US / own Allow at least one night between raid order and execution; prefer dawn or twilight; broad-daylight raids depend on smoke blinding all artillery observation.
    FM 7-20 Infantry Battalion, 1944, leaf 185, p. 181, para 198a
  129. c-USA04-0002 US / own Supporting infantry normally forms the base of fire for tank maneuver, then reduces resistance tanks cannot reach; battalion commander sets its mission, not its fire.
    FM 17-33 Armored Force Field Manual The Armored Battalion, leaf 18,19, p. 14-15, para 10
  130. c-USA04-0042 US / own Tanks need not attack first; infantry often secures launching ground or, with engineers, clears paths through obstacles beforehand.
    FM 17-33 Armored Force Field Manual The Armored Battalion, leaf 70, p. 66, para 28b
  131. c-USA04-0077 US / own Against light resistance, carried infantry leads the third echelon with tanks 200 to 500 yards behind; when fire dismounts it, tanks attack at once. 200 yd, 500 yd
    FM 17-33 Armored Force Field Manual The Armored Battalion, leaf 107, p. 103, para 35d(3)(a)
  132. c-USA04-0113 US / own Armored infantry rides until enemy fire or terrain forces dismounting, then fights afoot; vehicle weapons support from dispersed defilade; mines and obstacles hamper mounted movement.
    FM 17-42 Armored Infantry Battalion, 1944, leaf 4,5, p. 1-2, para 3c
  133. c-USA04-0114 US / own Primary role is action with tanks: follow their attack mopping up, hold ground won, seize launching terrain, form base of fire, clear mine lanes.
    FM 17-42 Armored Infantry Battalion, 1944, leaf 5,6, p. 2-3, para 4
  134. c-USA04-0115 US / own Part fires while the rest maneuvers, down to rifle squad; concentrate on critical areas, not simultaneous attacks on objectives far apart (figure: 5,000 yards). 5000 yd
    FM 17-42 Armored Infantry Battalion, 1944, leaf 6,8, p. 3, 5, para 5b-c, fig 3
  135. c-USA04-0116 US / own A corridor favors attack; take its limiting features first, include them in the unit's zone, and align unit boundaries with corridor boundaries.
    FM 17-42 Armored Infantry Battalion, 1944, leaf 12, p. 9, para 6b(2)(a)
  136. c-USA04-0119 US / own In attack, plan to seize dominating ridges and hilltops, advancing from one commanding feature to the next along covered routes.
    FM 17-42 Armored Infantry Battalion, 1944, leaf 13,14, p. 10-11, para 6c(1)
  137. c-USA04-0121 US / own Control passes to subordinates once attack starts, depending on prior arrangement; centralized control returns during reorganization with counterattack fires planned, and holds throughout defense.
    FM 17-42 Armored Infantry Battalion, 1944, leaf 20,21, p. 17-18, para 11c
  138. c-USA04-0122 US / own Infantry and tank commanders coordinate the tank mission with fire and maneuver, picking tank positions and alternate plans for either tanks or infantry to lead.
    FM 17-42 Armored Infantry Battalion, 1944, leaf 21, p. 18, para 12b
  139. c-USA04-0144 US / own Half-track armor stops small arms up to close range and fragments, but not antitank weapons or direct hits from assault guns and light artillery.
    FM 17-42 Armored Infantry Battalion, 1944, leaf 66,69, p. 63, 66, para 30d
  140. c-USA04-0148 US / own In a meeting engagement commit the battalion promptly, aggressiveness often deciding; when one is likely, supporting weapons are often decentralized to rifle companies.
    FM 17-42 Armored Infantry Battalion, 1944, leaf 74, p. 71, para 42b(1)
  141. c-USA04-0149 US / own When the enemy wants to break off, use full maneuverability to encircle, attack continuously to prevent consolidation, never lose contact, and use vehicular machine guns.
    FM 17-42 Armored Infantry Battalion, 1944, leaf 75, p. 72, para 42b(2)
  142. c-USA04-0150 US / own Against an organized position, plan coordination in detail as time allows, give supporting weapons definite missions, and begin with deliberate probing and neutralizing before assault.
    FM 17-42 Armored Infantry Battalion, 1944, leaf 75, p. 72, para 42b(3)
  143. c-USA04-0151 US / own Battalion seeks envelopment and suits a large force's flank; interior battalions start frontally, exploiting flank chances; narrowing the zone of action increases attack power.
    FM 17-42 Armored Infantry Battalion, 1944, leaf 75, p. 72, para 43a, 43c
  144. c-USA04-0152 US / own Part of the battalion often makes a secondary attack to deceive the enemy about the main attack, and it may become the main attack.
    FM 17-42 Armored Infantry Battalion, 1944, leaf 76, p. 73, para 43d
  145. c-USA04-0153 US / own Some vehicles fire from defilade; other assault company vehicles wait covered to the rear under platoon NCOs, covering flanks by fire; reserve retains vehicles.
    FM 17-42 Armored Infantry Battalion, 1944, leaf 76, p. 73, para 43e
  146. c-USA04-0155 US / own Reserve varies from one platoon to two companies, to repel counterattacks, replace exhausted elements, exploit weaknesses, or strike the final blow.
    FM 17-42 Armored Infantry Battalion, 1944, leaf 78, p. 75, para 46d
  147. c-USA04-0156 US / own Battalion generally attacks in a zone 500 to 1,000 yards wide, two rifle companies with supporting elements forward and the third in reserve. 500 yd, 1000 yd
    FM 17-42 Armored Infantry Battalion, 1944, leaf 78, p. 75, para 46e-f
  148. c-USA04-0157 US / own Help delayed units by shifting supporting fire; never hold an advanced unit for alignment, but protect it by moving supporting weapons and reserve forward.
    FM 17-42 Armored Infantry Battalion, 1944, leaf 80, p. 77, para 51b
  149. c-USA04-0158 US / own Reserve exploits success rather than redeems failure except in emergency; commit it whole against the enemy's weak point, never piecemeal, keeping it within supporting distance.
    FM 17-42 Armored Infantry Battalion, 1944, leaf 80, p. 77, para 51d

battalion / infantry / defense

Battalion defense

closed worksall-aroundreverse slopedepthinfiltration watch

A battalion holds closed works ready for all-around fire, about twice its attack width, in depth. Use reverse slopes. Build effect before cover: trenches, wire, MG and AT positions come first. Watch the gaps by observers and patrols, because infiltration comes through them.

GERITJPSUUKUS

How it works, with numbers

Base the defense on fortified closed works organized for all-around defense. Holding successive lines disperses force and suits only delay. c-USI12-0117

Reported of the Germans: normal sector 880 to 2,200 yards, part of a rule that defense roughly doubles attack width. c-GER-0032

Soviet: sector up to 2 km wide and 1.5 to 2 km deep; up to 5 km in difficult terrain, with separated company areas. SU02-0001 SU02-0027

Reported of the Japanese: 800 to 2,000 yards normally, up to 3,000 on a broad front, with supports and local reserves making 700 to 1,500 yards of depth. JP01-0131 JP01-0133

US depth: a battalion area runs up to 1,200 yards. The printed minimum in the same passage looks misread. c-USI12-0121

Reported of the Germans: reverse slopes wherever possible, since forward slopes are spotted early and invite massed fire. c-GER-0037

Reported of the Germans: work order follows effect before cover. Trenches, wire, MG and AT positions first; observation posts and heavy weapons next; artillery, AT ditches and dummies last. c-GER-0038

Against infiltration: daylight observers in each defense area watch the ground between them, and roving combat patrols search what they cannot see. c-USI17-0153

UK: a belt of fire of all arms in front of the foremost localities, fire in depth behind it. c-UK-3007

Soviet: when enemy fire unmasks a bunker, smoke it to spoil his fire correction. SU02-0033

Gaps: UK battalion defense rests on one 1937 line. Frontages are doctrine values, not game parameters.

Evidence: 311 claims, 3 held back

  63. c-USI17-0088 US / own Battalion main-line frontage: 1,000-2,000 yards; not over 1,000 in wooded broken ground; 1,500-2,000 in open; 2,500 on flat; 3,500 behind major obstacles. 1000 yd, 2000 yd, 1500 yd, 2500 yd, 3500 yd
    FM 7-20 Infantry Battalion, 1944, leaf 194, p. 190, para 209
  64. c-USI17-0089 US / own Battalion defense area depth runs 800-1,400 yards; all installations stay inside it except administrative ones, which need regimental approval. 800 yd, 1400 yd
    FM 7-20 Infantry Battalion, 1944, leaf 194, p. 190, para 209

    FM 7-20 Infantry Battalion, 1944, leaf 195, p. 191, para 210
  66. c-USI17-0091 US / own Defending while in contact: indicate only the general line, attach heavy machine guns and tanks to companies, then readjust into coordinated defense.

  67. c-USI17-0092 US / own Trace the main line for observation, concealment, denial of enemy observation, grazing flanking fire, obstacles and counterattack terrain; it may run on either slope.

  68. c-USI17-0093 US / own Make the main line irregular with minor salients and reentrants for flanking fire; avoid large ones; areas mutually support and defend all-around.

  69. c-USI17-0094 US / own Forward-slope positions keep observation and the best flat-trajectory fields, and cover obstacles by fire; extend company areas to the reverse slope for concealed routes.

  70. c-USI17-0095 US / own Choose reverse slope when exposed forward slope is untenable to observed fire, fields are better, salients must be avoided, or the forward slope is lost.

  78. c-USI17-0125 US / own If occupying under artillery or air attack, take concealed positions first; organize exposed ones after dark or by small-group infiltration.

    FM 7-20 Infantry Battalion, 1944, leaf 230, p. 226, para 226d
  88. c-USI17-0156 US / own Reserve battalion first prepares positions best protecting front battalions' flanks and rear and blocking most probable penetrations; may also outpost, assist digging, build dummies.

  90. c-USI17-0166 US / own If heavy air bombardment or armor might pin the reserve, regiment puts it in prepared defense areas to fire, hold, then reassemble for counterattack.

  91. c-USI17-0167 US / own Against infantry-artillery attack, reserve heavy weapons emplace for assigned missions; the rest waits in the assembly area, dispersed in foxholes; antitank platoon guards it.

  92. c-USI17-0169 US / own On a front too wide for mutual support, plan to shift weight rapidly against the main attack and form an all-around island, preparing several areas.

battalion / infantry / winter

Winter fighting

shelter groundski flankssnow worksslow off road

Thin evidence, Soviet only. Villages and woods matter more in winter, troops move slower off roads, and nights last longer. Deny the enemy shelter. Ski troops bypass and envelop. Without time to dig, build snow parapets; ice and charges go on tank approaches.

SU

How it works, with numbers

Soviet: villages and woods matter more in winter, movement without roads is slower and night fighting lasts longer. SU02-0268

Soviet: site defensive sectors to deny the enemy settlements and shelter. SU02-0066

Soviet: iced snow ramparts and charges on armored approaches; snow parapets when time is short. SU02-0067 SU02-0069

Soviet: skis for offensive action and flank counterattacks by defending battalions. Ski submachine gunners raid the rear, cutting communications and hitting transport and command posts. SU02-0068 SU03-0030

Soviet: ski troops bypass and envelop, with mortars and machine guns on sleds. A ski reserve counters enemy ski troops. SU02-0269 SU02-0272

Soviet: before attacking, learn snow depth and type and the best routes for tanks, infantry and guns. SU02-0271

Soviet: cut time in assembly and on the assault line; avoid long halts. Dummy works matter more in winter and get traps and mines. c-SU-2018 c-SU-2041

Gaps: Soviet only: one manual read in full plus checked second-pass reads. Finnish material is two pages. Stock game has no ski units; use for map-season flavor only.

battalion / infantry / withdrawal

Battalion delay and withdrawal

refuse close combatcrest then defiladerear guardawait dark

A delaying battalion refuses close combat, leaving before enemy rifle fire is effective, around 500 yards. Site the line near a crest: long fields of fire, immediate defilade behind. Two companies forward, one covering. Daylight disengagement is costly; wait for dark if allowed.

GERJPSUUKUS

How it works, with numbers

An independent delaying battalion refuses close combat against a coordinated superior attack, leaving before enemy rifle fire becomes effective, usually around 500 yards. c-USI18-0038

Site the delaying line near a topographical crest: long fields of fire forward, immediate defilade behind. c-USI18-0019

Two rifle companies on the first position, one as covering force; heavy weapons attach to the units they withdraw with. c-USI08-0045

Reported of the Germans: daylight disengagement cost heavily against Allied aircraft and armor, so troops wait for dark. If forced by day they withdraw by unit sectors, coordinating with neighbours. c-GER-0047

Reported of the Germans: a delaying battalion holds 1,750 to 4,400 yards with very little depth. A typical rear guard per route is one fresh infantry battalion, recon on the flanks and engineers for demolitions. c-GER-0055 c-GER-0048

Reported of the Germans: delay strongpoints stayed small. Close country took a gun or two with a pair of heavy mortars and about six MGs; open country a single gun with a few tanks and mounted infantry. c-GER-0059

Soviet: forward companies withdraw before a general assault, covered by the reserve and by rear guards on pre-arranged obstacles with AT weapons. SU02-0030

UK: withdraw step by step, each rear position organized before leaving the front one, with fresh troops holding it. Space delaying positions so the enemy must move his artillery forward again. UK07-0108 UK07-0107 UK04-0003

Reported of the Japanese: by night leave a shell of infantry with automatic weapons and small artillery. Withdraw when the enemy is within 1,000 yards. JP03-0038 JP02-0014

Soviet: leave a fight only by order and plan, best at night. By day break off under strong fire, flanking machine guns helping; heavy weapons fall back by bounds, sappers mine set lines. c-SU-2019 c-SU-2020 c-SU-2021

Soviet: at night or in fog all companies leave at once behind single platoons whose continued fire deceives the enemy. A rearguard fights whatever the losses. c-SU-2022 c-SU-2026

Soviet manoeuvre defense: two lines with AT ambushes between. The first fires long to force deployment, then leaves round the second, whose reserve covers it and counterattacks a break-in. c-SU-2027 c-SU-2028 c-SU-2029 c-SU-2030

Night disengagement: reported Japanese practice leaves a thin shell of infantry and automatic weapons, expected to sacrifice itself; Soviets may first make a short counterattack. JP03-0038 JP02-0005 SU03-0052

Gaps: Daylight and air limits rarely apply in a match, so the crest and early-leave rules matter most. In game, retreat settings (vanilla retreat_ratio, the overhaul mod's no_retreat) only steer idle units on AI auto-move; any withdraw order overrides them, so the withdrawal itself is always an order from above. Soviet manoeuvre defense and break-off read from BUP-2 (2026-11-08).

battalion / infantry / woods

Fighting in woods

edge is a targetshort haltsclose reserverush or infiltrate

Woods shorten fire to 10 to 100 yards and break control. Keep the reserve within 300 to 500 yards. Don't linger at an edge: guns target it. Reorganize short of the far edge, then leave in one rush if shelled, or by infiltration under small-arms fire.

GERJPSUUKUS

How it works, with numbers

Much woods fire is at 10 to 100 yards. Defenders offset poor observation with mines, booby traps and arranged fires, so aggressive reconnaissance is essential. c-USI17-0010

Attack the near edge under smoke or darkness when the approach is exposed. Keep the near-edge halt minimal, because artillery and aviation target that edge. c-USI17-0009 c-USI17-0008

Two companies abreast on a wide zone; one forward and two echeloned back gives the best flank security. c-USI17-0011

Reserve within 300 to 500 yards of leading rifle elements, by visibility. Small detachments guard AT guns and mortars. c-USI17-0017

Halt briefly at cross trails, streams or clearing edges to restore direction and contact; failing those, by timetable or azimuth distance. c-USI17-0018

Reorganize short of the far edge, deep enough to avoid fire on that edge. Debouch in one rush if artillery is the danger, and infiltrate if small arms are worse. c-USI17-0020 c-USI17-0021

Reported of the Germans: troops close to the edge, then all rush out together at least 100 yards before seeking cover. c-GER-0069

Soviet: bypass strong woodland points and leave them to follow-on forces, seize salients at the edge, and in large woods go clearing to clearing and trail to trail. SU02-0252 SU01-0283 SU01-0285

Defense in woods is weak in fields of fire, control, observation and communication. So use a strong rifle line, constant patrols, rapid reserve shifts and shorter distances. c-USA05-0033

Soviet defense: trace the main line in zigzag inside the woods for crossfire over lanes, with the reserve in an all-round strongpoint at road junctions. SU02-0060 SU02-0061

Soviet: move as a diamond with all-round security at least 100 m out; check side tracks to 400 m. Move silently, then fire and an immediate bayonet charge. c-SU-2010 c-SU-2012

Soviet: fix defenders of a large clearing frontally and bypass on the sides, with a reserve against counter-envelopment; in swamp woods, fights turn on defiles. c-SU-2011 c-SU-2013

UK jungle: high ground loses value since only treetops are seen; low ground hides positions better. c-UK-3009

Reported Japanese: guns on the infantry flanks fired as close as 55 yards ahead of the advance. c-JP-3003

UK wood clearing: ring the wood with fire, Bren groups hidden on every exit; beat through in a direction set by the enemy’s objective, the wood’s shape and a killing ground beyond. c-UK-3017 c-UK-3018

Gaps: UK and Japanese jungle practice not synthesized. German rule is reported. Soviet woods lines read from BUP-2.

battalion / tank / attack

Tank battalion attack

kill AT firstnot aloneechelonstandoff

Massed tanks do not break an effective AT screen alone. Neutralize AT guns first, then automatic weapons. Echelon on a narrow front so the commander can see and still has a reserve. Against weaker guns, stand off beyond his range and inside yours.

GERITJPSUUKUS

How it works, with numbers

Reported of the Germans, from costly experience: massed tanks cannot break an effective AT screen without other arms, and tank duels fail without superior range and armament. c-GER-0016

Order of work: first neutralize AT guns, then automatic weapons. Artillery fires on likely gun areas; supporting weapons watch to hit any flash or blast. c-USI12-0098

Against inferior armament, halt beyond his effective range and inside yours, and fire. If he advances, withdraw to keep the margin. c-USA04-0084

Reported of the Germans: battalions usually echelon one behind another, on about 1,100 yards of front. Two abreast spread too wide, and the commander can neither observe them nor commit anything of his own. c-GER-0018 c-GER-0019

Reported of the Germans: waves, now often two: the first speeds through to the guns, the second crushes forward positions and mops up. c-GER-0020

Launching tanks while foot troops are already attacking is the exception. It needs a route clear of the rifle lines, a defined tank zone and informed infantry. c-USI12-0091

Soviet: tanks stay within 200 to 400 m of their infantry. Short of transport, carry riflemen on the tanks and tow AT guns to keep them together in pursuit. SU02-0212 SU02-0285

Reported of the Japanese: infantry covers the tanks and holds ground they overrun; tanks are held in reserve under the division commander. JP03-0056 JP03-0053

Limits: heavy woods, stumps, steep rocky slopes, deep streams and soft ground. Reconnoiter; even when stopped, tank fire stays usable. c-USI16-0113

Reported German: a tank platoon is a command tank plus two pairs, in file, double file, wedge or blunt wedge; regiments attack in waves. c-GER-3003

Gaps: The UK tank battalion lines found were ammunition and organization, so UK is absent. German lines are reported, not German own text.

company / assault-gun / attack

Assault guns and tank destroyers

main effortcarry the infantry throughnot for close combatown security

Assault guns go to the main effort to help the infantry through. Tank destroyers are poor in close combat against infantry and need their own all-round security and early warning of tanks. Both can help reduce bunkers.

GERUS

How it works, with numbers

Reported German practice: assault guns are committed at the main effort, where they help the infantry penetrate. c-GER-3019

US: tank destroyers fare badly at close quarters with strong infantry; they keep their own all-round security, and warning of tanks is essential. Reducing bunkers is a secondary task. c-US-3003 c-US-3004

Gaps: Soviet self-propelled gun doctrine is not sourced in this pass. In game, the role comes from unit data (assault gun, tank destroyer).

company / engineer / assault

Pillbox and bunker assault

fire on embrasuressmokecut a laneflame and chargeswatch the exits

Find the pillbox by its embrasures and where it can flank the approach. Guns and machine guns hold its embrasures, smoke blinds it, a wire party cuts a lane, then the assault party closes with flame and charges. Others bypass it and watch its exits. When it falls silent, the attack goes on at once.

GERJPSUUS

How it works, with numbers

Soviet: pillboxes sit where they flank the approaches; find them by embrasures, camouflage and the muffled sound of their fire. c-SU-3023

Soviet assault group: two rifle sections, heavy MGs, anti-tank rifles, light mortars, one or two guns and sappers. Guns take the embrasures, sappers cut lanes, sections bypass and watch the exits, and the attack resumes once it is silent. c-SU-3006 c-SU-3007

Reported German practice: craters for cover; a machine gun on the embrasures from a flank, smoke laid by the wind, a wire party with bangalores, then the flamethrower. c-GER-3015 c-GER-3016

Soviet flamethrowers reach about 30 m and burn out MG nests, embrasures, trenches, tanks and stone buildings. c-SU-3009

US: tank destroyers are poor in close combat against strong infantry, but reducing bunkers is a secondary task. c-US-3003

The defender’s side, as reported: Japanese bunker entrances are angled or walled against grenades; German works are spaced so fire missing one does not hit another. c-JP-3008 c-GER-3017

Gaps: In game, pillboxes are map objects or static guns, and flame and charges are unit weapons per mod. UK own pillbox drill is not in this pass.

Engineers and obstacles in defense

covered obstaclestandoffguard the workstaged works

Thin evidence. An obstacle must be covered by fire; without it, mines only delay briefly. Keep it at least 50 m from your trenches to stay out of grenade range. A covering party protects the working party.

company / infantry / ambush

Ambush

close groundlet scouts passleader opensstaggered sidesleave fast

Lay the ambush in close ground on the enemy’s approach, on both sides of the route but staggered so no one hits his own. Let the scouts pass; the leader opens with rapid fire, best shots on leaders, men told off for vehicles. Strike hard, take prisoners, and leave before he recovers.

JPSUUKUS

How it works, with numbers

Soviet section ambush: close ground on enemy approaches, surprise fire at close range, then the bayonet; speed and surprise decide, prisoners are the aim. c-SU-3003

Reported British practice: the leader opens fire; fire is rapid for shock; the best shots take officers and NCOs; scouts are let through. c-UK-3022

Reported British practice: stagger parties on both sides of the track so they cannot hit each other; high ground helps, but a downhill flight escapes faster. c-UK-3023

UK: by day, reserve or mobile infantry ambush small tank groups. US: mines in an ambush block the lead and rear tanks. c-UK-3010 c-US-3002

Reported Japanese practice: jungle ambushes and road blocks against road-bound columns. c-JP-3004

Gaps: The overhaul mod's RecognizeTime 0.01 makes spotting near instant, so ambush surprise is weaker than in vanilla. German own ambush doctrine is not sourced.

company / infantry / approach

Company approach march

covered columnspread by daybound terrainclear the road

Stay concealed and in column as long as covered ground allows. By day separate platoons, up to 300 yards on open ground. Bound between terrain features 500 to 600 yards apart. On air or tank warning clear the road and disperse.

GERITJPSUUKUS

How it works, with numbers

Soviet: the company reaches its line concealed, without losses and on direction. With covered approaches it stays in column as long as possible. c-SU-0035

US: by day platoons separate laterally, in depth or both, up to 300 yards on open terrain, while the company keeps control. UK: about 200 yards apart. c-USI03-0076 UK03-0040

Intermediate objectives are terrain features, preferably 500 to 600 yards apart, that protect the force and cover its preparations. c-USI03-0084

On air or tank warning foot troops clear the road, disperse and use holes, ditches and tank obstacles. Carriers leave the probable impact area. c-USI03-0062

Soviet: a company in fog must react at once to contact at very short range. When the situation outruns orders, the commander acts on his own initiative. SU05-0074 SU01-0010

Soviet: submachine gunners with obstacle-clearing teams infiltrate the security zone and strike from behind to speed the advance. SU02-0217

Reported of the Japanese: an advance guard gets enemy and terrain information, protects deployment and seizes key ground. In jungle, flank patrols lose much of their value. JP01-0061 JP02-0057

Reported of the Germans: infantry warn assault guns of obstacles and mines and guide them through, and stay spread out near them to reduce exposure to fire and ricochets. GER04-0022 GER04-0024

Soviet: a head outpost 1 to 2 km ahead; AT guns lead the column. On tank alarm, companies split, infantry shelter behind tank-proof ground, guns deploy. c-SU-2023 c-SU-2024 c-SU-2025

Reported of the Japanese: a blocked advance guard deploys, or pretends to, and finds flanks and heavy weapons while the main body moves round. c-JP-2001 c-JP-2002

Gaps: Doctrine yard values describe wartime marches; a match needs only the order: concealed column, then spread, then deploy.

company / infantry / attack

Company attack

main effortcovered groundtwo up one backsupport held

Don't advance evenly. Push part of the company through the best-covered ground into a weak spot while the rest press and split the enemy's effort. Usually two platoons lead and one is held back. An interior company's zone is 200 to 500 yards, at most what its leaders can control.

GERITJPSUUKUS

How it works, with numbers

An even advance across the whole front, ignoring ground and enemy, is unlikely to succeed. Positions are rarely held evenly: open salients are thin, broken ground and covered reentrants stronger. c-US-1009 c-US-1008

Main effort: one portion goes through the best-covered ground against a weak spot. The others press by fire and movement over the next-best ground, so the enemy has to divide his defense. c-US-1010 c-US-1011

Formation follows the situation. Two up, one back is commonest. One up, two back suits a narrow zone, an exposed flank or an unclear enemy. All abreast is exceptional. The British rule agrees: the fewest platoons forward that the task allows. c-US-1004 c-US-1005 c-US-1006 c-UK-1001

Numbers: US company zone 200 to 500 yards, platoon 100 to 200. British manuals refuse a fixed rule and cap frontage by control. Too narrow is also wrong, because bunching costs room and raises losses. c-US-1007 c-US-1012 c-UK-1009 c-UK-1010 c-UK-1012

A frontal attack is quicker to organize but meets the enemy's best-prepared direction. A flank attack is likelier to decide it but takes longer and needs the ground. c-UK-1006 c-UK-1007

Every move is covered by fire. Riflemen shouldn't grind out what supporting weapons could finish. c-US-1003 c-US-1027

A unit not stopped keeps going although neighbors are halted, which outflanks what holds them. Weak spots and gaps get pressed hard. Failed platoon attacks still reveal enemy positions. c-US-1026 c-UK-1008 c-UK-1021

Reserve: don't spend it piecemeal. Commit it at once for a decisive blow or to restart a stalled attack, preferably at a flank or where weakness showed, not against strong resistance. Then rebuild one from relieved platoons and strays. c-US-1014 c-US-1035 c-US-1037 c-US-1038 c-US-1039 c-UK-1018 c-UK-1020

Reported, not German doctrine in its own words: attacks mass on a narrow Schwerpunkt, with weaker diversionary forces elsewhere, and a company sector runs about 330 to 550 yards. The same report warns the Germans repeat the same maneuvers. c-GER-0008 c-GER-0011 c-GER-0001

Soviet: a company also attacks on 200 to 500 meters. After a simultaneous first rush, platoons take firing lines in turn, halted platoons covering the movers. A failed assault digs in, regroups and goes again without waiting for help. c-SU-0036 c-SU-0037 c-SU-0041

UK: strong static defences need mixed sapper and infantry groups; attack silently at night if surprise is possible, else under intense covering fire. c-UK-3005

Gaps: Soviet comes from the Red Army infantry regulations, undated in this copy, in mediocre OCR. UK company attack comes from 1937 Infantry Training; Part VIII of 1944 covers only section and platoon. German is reported through a US manual.

Evidence: 847 claims, 2 held back

company / infantry / counterattack

Counterattack

before he organizesflankplannedstop at the line

A penetration is fought at once by the support, by fire or by counterattack, and it must land before the enemy organizes. It strikes his flank in maximum force, while fires across the base of the penetration stop more from entering. Pursuit past the old line is by fire only.

GERJPSUUKUS

How it works, with numbers

The company support fights a penetration by fire or by counterattack, the commander's choice, and it must land before the enemy organizes. c-USD-0029

Plans are made in advance: battalion names assumed penetrations and the reserve prepares against them. Walk the leaders over the ground at least. c-USD-0030 c-USD-0033

Strike the flank in maximum force. Objectives stay within the battalion area. Pursuit past the main line is by fire only. c-USD-0031

Mass weapons platoon, cannon, heavy weapons and artillery across the base of the penetration. c-USD-0032

Platoon level: the support platoon retakes a lost area with a quick assault on the flank, using the whole platoon. c-USD-0057 c-USD-0058

Hold a reserve company back while a hostile mechanized attack is still an immediate threat. c-USD-0034

Attackers should expect this. Infantry is most vulnerable to tanks just after taking an objective, while reorganizing. c-UK-1032

Reported of the Germans: a lost position gets artillery fire first, and nearby infantry and support weapons counterthrust immediately behind it, preferably at the flanks. c-GER-0044

Soviet: the reserve platoon stands 150 to 300 meters behind the forward strongpoints, clear of shelling aimed at them. On a break-in everything fires, then the commander counterattacks at once into the flank. Pursuit usually stops at the forward edge. c-SU-0056 c-SU-0058 c-SU-0060

UK: the reserve company is ready at short notice to form a defensive flank or counter-attack. c-UK-3008

Reported German: counterattack reserves wait sheltered and go in fresh as a unit, once the attack loses momentum and before it reorganises; the best assault troops are kept for it. c-GER-3006 c-GER-3007

Soviet: the reserve company strikes suddenly into flank and rear, short and sharp, to a set depth; a reserve tank company waits dug in with assigned sectors. c-SU-3016 c-SU-3018

Gaps: British counterattack rests on a training-pamphlet line. Soviet is in mediocre OCR.

company / infantry / deception

Bait and deception

baitdummiesfeinthold fireambush

Make the enemy show himself with a bait, such as a dummy, decoy, feint, noise or a weapon firing to provoke a reply, then kill what answered with a hidden weapon. Refuse his bait. Only named guns engage decoys and scouts, and the rest hold to the set range. Dummies work only if plausible and well clear of real works.

GERJPSUUKUS

How it works, with numbers

US dummies: plausible, where real works could stand, 150 yards or more from any real one, and manned during enemy reconnaissance. A recognised dummy tells the enemy where you are not. c-USI06-0166 c-USI17-0130 c-USI12-0174 c-USA02-0071

US anti-tank discipline: the enemy uses feints, decoys, dummy tanks and fighting reconnaissance to draw early fire. Only named guns engage them; the rest hold for the set range or line. c-USI09-0046 c-USI11-0031 c-USI10-0025 c-USI10-0017

US lures: light tanks draw the enemy into prepared traps; tanks caught by heavier ones lure them onto supporting mediums. One gun stays silent through the fight and opens after the platoon has gone. c-USA03-0168 c-USA03-0139 c-USA03-0020

US feints: part of a battalion attacks to mislead about the main attack and may become it; armoured cars feint while dismounted scouts identify. c-USA04-0152 c-USA02-0016 c-USA03-0167

Withdrawal cover. US: a covering force of single guns and mortars keeps up normal fire, radio and flares while the rest leaves. Soviet: single platoons' fire deceives. US recon: one section makes noise. c-USI17-0215 c-USI18-0013 c-SU-2022 c-USA02-0027

US: rapid single shots hide automatic weapons and make rifle strength look greater. c-USI02-0044

Ambush. Soviet: closed ground, close surprise fire then bayonet, a way out ready; tanks wait in weakened wooden buildings. US: hit tanks at defiles, bridges and fords; tank destroyers ambush and never chase. UK: an ambush party on the village's line of retreat. c-SU-0001 c-SU-2039 c-USA-0040 c-USA-0048 UK01-0144 UK01-0146

German snipers: if no target shows, lure fire with a helmet or straw dummy; if the enemy grows careful, rest the sector for days. c-GER-2001 c-GER-2002 GER01-0013

Reported of the Japanese: a noisy frontal show with firecrackers fakes strength while the main force envelops; light machine gun fire baits hidden heavy weapons, which mortars then hit; a blocked advance guard may only pretend to deploy. c-JP-2003 c-JP-2004 c-JP-2002

Soviet: dummy works matter more in winter and carry traps and mines; ruse and deception are needed for any task. c-SU-2041 c-SU-2044

UK: a platoon fakes its axis with smoke across the front and a few men recrossing a gap on one flank while two sections attack the other; in defense, alternative posts mislead. UK01-0021 UK02-0011

Roving guns (German, reported) and roving mortars (Soviet) fire from shifting spots to hide true positions; Soviet dummy positions sit where fire on them cannot hit real ones. GER03-0009 SU01-0158 SU02-0020

Soviet: do not commit the reserve to a demonstration. Reported Japanese practice pairs a noisy front demonstration with a silent flank march. SU03-0008 JP02-0071

Reported German infiltrators hide for days, then at the attack make the defender think he is surrounded. c-GER-3008

Gaps: UK and German own deception doctrine is thin; the leads were checked against the page (2026-11-08) and are now cited. Air deception left out as not in the game.

company / infantry / defense

Company defense

stop by firedepthblock approacheshold fire

Stop the enemy by fire ahead of the line, and meet those who arrive in close combat. Two platoons forward and one in support, positions covering each other in width and depth. Frontage runs from 500 yards in close ground to 800 to 1,000 in the open, about double an attack zone.

GERJPSUUKUS

How it works, with numbers

The forward company halts the enemy by fire ahead of the main line, and close combat repels whoever reaches it. The layout covers the front, trades support with neighbors, shields supporting weapons, spreads in width and depth and resists all round. c-USD-0001 c-USD-0002

Numbers: at most 500 yards in vital close ground, 800 to 1,000 in the open, garrisons 150 to 500 yards apart in depth: inside rifle range, outside artillery fire aimed at the neighbor. c-USD-0003 c-USD-0004 c-USD-0005

Usually two platoons on the line and one in support. By day platoons block the covered approaches and machine guns cover the open ground between. At night they swap, because the enemy then uses the open. c-USD-0006 c-USD-0007 c-USD-0008

One leader owns each avenue of approach. The commander finds where heavy fires land, then fills gaps with rifles and light mortars. c-USD-0010 c-USD-0016

Fire: long-range weapons engage first. Riflemen stay in cover through the preparation and hold fire to effective range, 500 yards, then everything opens. Close in, guns go to final protective lines. c-USD-0024 c-USD-0021 c-USD-0025

Reserve lies on rear key terrain 150 to 500 yards behind the forward support. When a neighbor is penetrated it holds a flank line or counterattacks. c-USD-0027 c-USD-0028

Anti-tank: keep mines and obstacles under fire. Grenadiers hunt armor while other infantry weapons hold fire at tanks. c-USD-0017 c-USD-0018

Reported of the Germans: a company defends 440 to 1,100 yards, roughly double the attack width, and uses reverse slopes wherever possible because forward slopes get spotted and destroyed. c-GER-0031 c-GER-0032 c-GER-0037

Soviet: a company area runs up to 1,000 meters wide and deep, with the forward edge swept at 200 to 400 by frontal, flanking and oblique fire. Fire should not be even: mass it suddenly on the densest attackers, then shift just as suddenly. c-SU-0054 c-SU-0055 c-SU-0057

Soviet: be ready for enemy smoke: move from depth when it starts and fire extra tasks on approaches. c-SU-2042

Gaps: Soviet comes from the Red Army infantry regulations, undated in this copy, in mediocre OCR. British defense is not read yet.

company / infantry / infiltration

Infiltration and its counter

no preparationdark or fogunwatched groundall-round postshunting reserves

Small, heavily armed groups slip through unwatched or "impassable" ground, often in darkness or fog, while the main attack holds the defender. They take the start line or strike from behind. The counter is self-contained posts that fight all round, used as pivots for reserves that hunt the infiltrators.

GERJPSUUS

How it works, with numbers

Reported German practice: attacks without artillery preparation for surprise, in darkness or fog; the start line is occupied by infiltration to save losses. c-GER-3012

Reported Soviet practice: units with submachine guns, a mortar and a machine gun cross unguarded or impassable ground while the main assault pins the defense. c-SU-3022

Soviet: submachine gunners infiltrate enemy formations, lay ambushes, guard flanks and rear, and kill enemy infiltrators. c-SU-3004

Reported Japanese practice: one or two light machine gunners left in the rear had a strong psychological effect. c-JP-3005

US: the best counter is posts that can hold alone and fire in every direction, anchoring reserves that strike hard. c-US-3005

Gaps: UK own infiltration doctrine is not sourced. In game, infiltration needs routes outside enemy sight; read the map’s cover and vision.

company / infantry / night

Night attack

recon firststraight aheadsilenthedgehog at halt

Reconnoiter at least the night before. Go straight at the objective: mixing frontal attack and envelopment at night usually produces confusion and friendly fire. Stay in column until 100 to 200 yards out, silent and marked. Units stopped by darkness dig in all-round.

GERJPSUUKUS

How it works, with numbers

Stay in platoon columns as long as practicable. Deploy as skirmishers only 100 to 200 yards out, before sentries can see. c-USI04-0007

US pace: about 1 mile an hour cross-country to the forward assembly area, then 100 yards per 6 to 10 minutes. c-USI04-0012

Combining frontal attack and envelopment at night usually yields an uncoordinated assault and friendly conflict, so platoons attack straight ahead. c-USI04-0022

Patrols knock out listening posts and outguards just before the force reaches them. If challenged, scouts close with the bayonet and others lie down; the commander prevents a premature assault. c-USI04-0020 c-USI04-0025

One-company attack: give the order at least two hours before dark so subordinates can reconnoiter. c-USI16-0163

German: success depends on reconnaissance at least one night before. Move silently with no lights, use visual markers and go for flank or rear. GER01-0066 GER01-0103 GER01-0067

German: infiltrating units halted by darkness set up all-round defense and reorganize at dawn. GER01-0056

UK: rest and feed first, mark routes, and limit engagement to targets within 200 yards. Patrol constantly in the dark to watch the gaps. UK04-0156 UK04-0157 UK05-0209 UK04-0137

Soviet: in poor visibility narrow each weapon's sector and raise density on the front line. SU03-0137

Soviet: night defense keeps a duty subunit ready, weapons laid on approaches by day. A night counterattack is simple, short and prompt, before the enemy digs in. c-SU-2031 c-SU-2032

Gaps: Whether a map plays at night depends on the mission. Vision changes matter more in-game than the doctrine timings.

company / infantry / pursuit

Pursuit

at onceno waitingbroad frontcut the retreatguns forward

When the enemy breaks, pursue at once without waiting for neighbours. Press on a broad front against his flanks, take the shortest routes to cut his retreat, and push guns and machine guns forward so he cannot re-form. Bypass obstacles and cut off rearguards. Only a senior commander halts it.

SU

How it works, with numbers

Soviet: pursuit is relentless, led by bold small units, especially submachine gunners, with commanders at the head; only a senior commander halts it. c-SU-3011

Soviet: do not wait for neighbours; press on a broad front against the flanks and take the shortest routes to cut the retreat. c-SU-3012

Soviet: guns, heavy MGs and mortars push forward so the enemy cannot form columns; bypass obstacles, cut off rearguards, no halts at intermediate lines. c-SU-3013

The counterattack limit applies too: Soviet reserve companies pursue only to a set depth, usually the forward edge. c-SU-3016

Gaps: Pursuit here is Soviet doctrine only; other nations were not searched deeply.

company / infantry / reverse-slope

Reverse-slope defense

behind the crestoutposts forwardcrest is the killing groundcounterattack the crest

When the enemy can watch the forward slope, put the main position behind the crest. Outposts hold the forward slope; heavy weapons and most troops wait behind and fire onto the crest as the enemy tops it. Woods give the same cover. The risk: lose the crest and you lose the view.

GERSUUKUS

How it works, with numbers

US: the main line goes on the reverse slope when enemy observed fire would make the forward slope untenable. c-US-3001

Reported German practice: outposts on the forward slope, heavy weapons behind the crest, most of the unit held for counterattack; guns on a second ridge fire onto the first crest once it falls. c-GER-3010 c-GER-3009

UK: company localities give all-round fire, usually on reverse slopes. c-UK-3012

Soviet: a reverse-slope trench is hidden from ground observers and has covered communications, but the enemy dominates it once he holds the crest. c-SU-3001

Woods work like a reverse slope (reported German). Soviet: sit back from the wood edge or forward of it, never on it, so artillery cannot range the edge. c-GER-3011 c-SU-3002

Reported German heavy mortars sit on reverse slopes. c-GER-3020

Gaps: In game, sight lines come from map height; the crest rule needs that data per map. Japanese reverse-slope practice is not sourced here.

company / infantry / river

River crossing

surprisethree abreastalternate pointsrally far bank

Lead companies cross by boat, reserves by bridge. Form boat groups early and keep tactical unity. Normally three platoons abreast, with weapons following once they land. Hold fire on the water, rally on prominent features, clear the bank fast. Advance guards may simply cross by surprise.

SUUKUS

How it works, with numbers

Leading rifle companies cross in assault boats, reserves by bridge or ferry. c-USI04-0050

Form boat groups before leaving the rear area and keep tactical unity. The infantry who cross carry their boats; engineers control movement from final assembly. c-USI04-0054

No firing from boats in darkness, no paddling against drift unless ordered, and alternate crossing points for succeeding waves. c-USI04-0057

Usually all three rifle platoons cross side by side. Heavier weapons and the commander's group go over once they have landed. c-USI04-0058

Boatloads rally on prominent features and clear the bank promptly. In darkness hold fire and close with the bayonet. c-USI04-0059

Advance guards and pursuing detachments often cross by surprise using whatever is at hand. c-USI04-0064

Without boats: swim with logs and rafts, and ferry vital equipment and ammunition on improvised floats. c-USI17-0057

Soviet: existing bridges, wading, boats or winter ice; near the enemy, fords and issued boats. SU04-0109 SU04-0110

UK: know wind and current before shoving off, and keep extra bridging at assembly points to replace losses. UK01-0181 UK05-0107

Soviet: cross at night or dawn for surprise. The first wave is at least a rifle company with heavy machine guns, guns, AT rifles, observers and sappers. c-SU-2014 c-SU-2015

Soviet: picked AT riflemen seize the far bank first; the first wave holds a covering line until the whole battalion is across. c-SU-2016 c-SU-2017

Gaps: Few maps need a boat assault. The usable core: crossing points are chokes, cover the far bank first, and do not bunch. Soviet crossing lines read from BUP-2; German and UK river doctrine not read.
