company / infantry / smoke

Smoke

smoke on enemywindshort lifeHE if locatedcoordinate

Smoke goes on the enemy, not in front of yourself. US tests gave a four-to-one fire advantage that way. Wind decides: a steady light breeze is best, and wind blowing toward you rules it out except in withdrawal. Rounds last seconds to minutes, so time smoke to the move. Use HE on located targets and smoke on unlocated ones.

GERSUUKUS

How it works, with numbers

US: smoke on the enemy, not in front of the firer, gave a four-to-one fire advantage in tests; rifle fire suffers most. Lay it upwind of him. c-USA01-0017 c-USA03-0006 c-USA02-0109

US wind: best a steady 3 to 6 mph in cool, cloudy air. Above 10 mph it tears, below 3 it wanders; clear midday sky and woods are poor. Never smoke with the wind toward you unless withdrawing. c-USA01-0013 c-USA01-0016 c-USA03-0136

Short life. US: an 81-mm round smokes about half a minute; a 75-mm tank round screens 50 yards for about 10 seconds. UK: a 2-in. mortar bomb lasts some minutes, a grenade about 45 seconds; mortar smoke takes half a minute to build. c-USA01-0012 c-USA01-0074 c-UK-1043 c-UK-1044

US uses: screen moves, attacks and withdrawals; blind AT guns, automatic weapons and observers; cover breaching; mislead about the attack point. Daylight river crossings and raids go under smoke. c-USA01-0007 c-USI17-0050 c-USI04-0075 c-USI11-0125

US choice: HE on located targets in range, smoke on unlocated or out-of-range ones unless it hampers your own moves. A tank screens a suspected gun's field of view with smoke; once the assault is moving, located AT guns get HE. c-USA01-0029 c-USA01-0084 c-USA01-0052

US tanks on an emplacement: smoke on it and its neighbours, tanks rush, close infantry and engineers finish the crew; with the wind toward you, smoke only the neighbours. Caught by heavier tanks: smoke part, close fast with the rest. c-USA01-0137 c-USA01-0138 c-USA03-0139

UK: under severe flank fire, mortar smoke gives artificial defilade. Smoking the objective as the assault goes in also blinds the assaulters, and gaps can silhouette them. c-UK-1040 c-UK-1047

Coordinate and ration. US: one mortar in a cross wind can blind neighbours or hide the enemy from their fire; smoke is only about 20 percent of mortar shell carried, so screens stay small. c-USA03-0007 c-USA03-0135 c-USI06-0064

Soviet: mortars blind the enemy with smoke; a defender plans moves from depth and extra fire on approaches the moment enemy smoke starts. Reported of the Germans: smoke supplements other weapons, with more smoke candles than US practice. c-SU-2043 c-SU-2042 c-USI18-0048

Under enemy smoke, US: weapons on predetermined data keep firing and all heavy weapons lay on close defensive fires, so smoke alone does not stop a prepared defense. c-USI06-0185 c-USI07-0085

UK: grenade smoke lasts about 45 s; 2-inch mortar smoke lasts longer but takes half a minute to thicken. German Blendkörper on a tank: 15-20 s. c-UK-3001 GER01-0124

Smoke grenades on tank air inlets blind and sicken the crew before sticky bombs go on (UK). Reported German smoke parties screen pillbox assaults. UK02-0052 c-GER-3001

Gaps: German smoke is mostly reported. Japanese smoke doctrine was not found, only equipment lists. Wind does not move smoke in game (VIS-16) and smoke life is fixed per mod.

company / infantry / withdrawal

Delay and withdrawal

leave earlycover in turndouble frontagelong range

Leave before rifle fire pins you and before the enemy can assault. By day each echelon covers the last in turn. On a delaying position a company holds twice its normal frontage and opens at extreme range, 800 to 1,200 yards, to force deployment, then goes.

GERJPSUUKUS

How it works, with numbers

Withdraw before hostile rifle fire pins the troops and before the enemy gets within assaulting distance. c-USD-0044

Daylight: delaying actions on successive positions, each echelon covering the last. The support platoon covers the front line and the battalion reserve covers the front-line companies. c-USD-0037 c-USD-0038

A delaying company can hold twice the normal frontage, with three platoons abreast for fire power, because any one position offers only limited resistance. c-USD-0039 c-USD-0040

Fire: long range, opening at 800 to 1,200 yards, to make the enemy deploy and spend time. Choose a topographical crest, which gives defilade as soon as the troops leave. c-USD-0042 c-USD-0041

Night: a covering force, usually one squad per platoon plus single weapons, mimics normal activity and keeps patrolling so the enemy doesn't notice. c-USD-0035 c-USD-0036

Platoons leave successively with supporting weapons covering the gaps, or together, each covering itself. c-USD-0060

Reported of the Germans: the rearmost company rotates and retires through the others, leapfrogging until dark. Troops never retire from patrols, only from a mounted attack. c-GER-0049 c-GER-0057

Reported of the Germans: covering forces let the enemy no closer than their next line is distant, or losses become excessive. Strongpoints shift often and leave just before a full attack arrives. c-GER-0056 c-GER-0060

Soviet: intermediate lines lie no farther apart than effective heavy machine gun range. A fight on one never waits for the assault: after disrupting him by fire, units bound back under cover, the commander last. c-SU-0061 c-SU-0062 c-SU-0030

Reported German delay: flank tanks lure enemy armour to deploy and cover the AT guns’ withdrawal; SP guns shift position constantly behind them. GER04-0006

UK: a withdrawal needs preparation; every commander keeps it in mind, and discipline must hold. c-UK-3016

Soviet delay: hold intermediate lines without letting the enemy reach assault distance, withdraw by bounds under fire from depth; a section goes cover to cover, riflemen first, LMG and commander last. c-SU-3014 c-SU-3015

Gaps: British withdrawal is not read yet. Soviet is in mediocre OCR.

company / mg / attack

Machine guns and mortars in the attack

oblique firekeep firingshift at assaultsmall targets

Machine guns fire from a flank or obliquely, so the beaten zone lies along the target, and they stay in action. Just before the assault they get on the flank of the resistance, because they can fire after other weapons lift. Mortars are for small, known targets, since ammunition is scarce.

GERITJPSUUKUS

How it works, with numbers

Site guns for flanking or oblique fire. Frontal fire only when ground rules out anything else and it is essential. The British agree, and avoid overhead fire where they can. c-US-1019 c-US-1020 c-UK-1024 c-UK-1033

Guns are normally under company control. Attaching them to one platoon burdens its leader. A gun helps only when firing, so hold one back only for a definite purpose. c-US-1064 c-US-1021 c-UK-1027

Ammunition limits them, so concentrate on limited targets where they help most. c-US-1029

At the assault: get on the flank of the resistance beforehand. When masked, shift to enemy on the flanks of the assaulted position, without orders if needed. c-US-1030 c-US-1068

Displace only when the mission can't be done from where the gun is. Move by squads while riflemen advance. After a capture, guns go to cover the front and flanks against counterattack. c-US-1066 c-US-1067 c-US-1070

Mortars: a squad carries about two minutes of continuous fire. Fire at dug-in or defiladed targets clearly blocking the advance and known within about a 50-yard square. Never search large areas or fire at indefinite targets. c-US-1031 c-US-1032 c-US-1017

British: mortar high explosive decides only small targets such as located guns, not woods, crests or building groups. Mortars stay forward to fire at once, and reserves exploiting without a fire plan need them most. c-UK-1030 c-UK-1028 c-UK-1031

Mortars cover the final advance once other fires are masked, then shift to positions firing on the assault force. c-US-1033 c-US-1069

Reported of the Japanese: machine guns sit well forward in hidden pairs and open for maximum surprise. c-JP-2007

Soviet: fire support is continuous; some mortars, heavy MGs and guns bound forward with the infantry while the rest fire from depth. c-SU-3010

Gaps: Heavy machine guns and 81-mm mortars at battalion are not read yet. Stock AS2 has no suppression, so the value of fire here is a proxy.

company / mg / defense

Machine guns in defense

enfiladecrossing firefixed linesno gaps at flanks

The machine gun is the backbone of the defense. Site it for enfilade so its fire crosses a neighbour’s on fixed lines; heavy MGs lay interlocking final protective lines. Leave no gap in the belt of fire, especially at the flanks.

GERJPSUUKUS

How it works, with numbers

UK: the machine gun is the strongest defensive weapon, firing to about 2,000 yards even at obscured targets, best in enfilade. c-UK-3013

UK: defensive fire is crossing fire on fixed lines, and the belt has no gaps, especially at the flanks. c-UK-3014 c-UK-3015

US: interlocking final protective lines are a heavy machine gun task. c-US-3006

Reported German practice: a close-country strongpoint holds one or two SP guns, a pair of heavy mortars and as many as six MGs, firing all round. c-GER-3021

Gaps: Range figures are 1937 British; in game use the mod’s MG range from the profile.

company / mortar / attack

Company mortars in the attack

well forwardfire at oncesmall targetslift deep

Mortars keep the attack moving: well forward, firing at once on a located gun or defiled troops. High explosive decides only on small targets. Keep some for reserves that exploit. When the assault goes in, lift to depth and flanks to cut counterattacks.

GERITJPSUUKUS

How it works, with numbers

UK: restarting a stopped attack takes a new plan and usually new troops, so quick-support mortars stay well forward and fire immediately to keep momentum. They answer to forward company commanders and bound close to company headquarters. c-UK-1028 c-UK-1029

UK: high explosive is decisive only on small targets such as located machine guns or narrow defiles. Woods, crests and big groups of buildings are unsuitable. c-UK-1030

US: fire at defiladed guns, mortars or men clearly blocking the advance and known to lie within about a 50-yard square. c-US-1032

UK: with a programmed attack, reserve companies exploiting without arranged support often need mortars more than the forward companies, so some may be held back for them. c-UK-1031

US: keep fire superiority over forward positions during the final advance to assaulting distance, once other fires are masked. Turn on counterattacks to stop or delay them. c-US-1033 c-US-1034

Soviet: when the bayonet assault starts, shift to depth and flanks, separating counterattacking infantry from its tanks. Companies move up by platoons during deep penetration. SU02-0144 SU02-0149 SU02-0145

The US 60-mm is useful to 1,000 yards at up to 20 rounds a minute, for overhead and masked fire at defiladed targets close to the front. Economize ammunition. c-USI12-0037

The observation post must see both friendly troops and the target, within voice or arm-signal distance of the mortar. c-USI04-0206

Soviet: battalion mortars suppress machine guns and mortars and blind the enemy with smoke. c-SU-2043

Reported Japanese: the discharger squad fires its first rounds to the platoon leader’s plan, later rounds at the squad leader’s discretion. c-JP-3001

Reported German practice: heavy mortars sit on reverse slopes, with a trend toward concentrated fire. c-GER-3020

Gaps: German company mortar practice is reported only (TM-E 30-451, 1945); Japanese is reported. Distances are for the named weapons; use mod weapon ranges in the game.

company / tank / attack

Tank company attack, with infantry

envelopsupport firesassault togetherinfantry when mined

Envelop as the rule: support elements fire from the front while the company moves under cover to a flank or rear. Attack frontally only when forced. Against a fortified position or tank obstacles the infantry goes first. Leading platoons assault together, about 300 yards or less out, once anti-tank weapons are gone.

GERJPSUUKUS

How it works, with numbers

Envelopment is the usual method: support or the advance guard fires frontally while the company moves under cover. Frontal attack only when terrain rules out a flank, or against a weak, disorganized enemy when time is critical. c-USA-0024 c-USA-0023

Attack in depth when weak points are known, and in width when the situation is unclear. Column breaks through and turns outward. In line, two lead and one supports. c-USA-0031 c-USA-0032 c-USA-0033

Support fire intensifies before and during the first stages, then lifts as platoons close. Fire and movement continues until the position's anti-tank weapons are gone. The assault normally starts about 300 yards or less out. c-USA-0026 c-USA-0028

Leading platoons assault together; piecemeal gives away much of the effect. A failed attack rallies at the alternate point and goes again. c-USA-0027 c-USA-0029

Infantry: against a well-fortified position it goes first. When tanks lead, infantry exploits at once, because tanks waiting on the objective take losses. It doesn't divert to flanking resistance; reserves take that. c-USA-0030 c-UK-1022 c-UK-1023

Against tanks: never charge. Strike first with accurate fire from the halt, in cover, and ambush at defiles. Enemy tanks are most dangerous while you fight others or reorganize. c-USA-0036 c-USA-0038 c-USA-0040 c-USA-0037

A tank company lacks self-sufficiency: it normally fights within the battalion and sustains separate action only briefly. c-USA-0021

Reported of the Germans: tanks reach full value only once infantry kills the anti-tank weapons, and where tank obstacles exist infantry goes first. c-GER-0025 c-GER-0024

Reported of the Germans: massed tanks can't break an effective screen without other arms. Infantry bounds in small groups clear of individual tanks, which draw fire. c-GER-0016 c-GER-0026

Soviet, from the infantry side: with tanks the company may attack straight behind them, clearing anti-tank obstacles and suppressing anti-tank weapons. c-SU-0040

Reported German practice: tanks hull-down on a ridge pin with machine guns while antitank and infantry guns kill the defending guns; tanks go in fully only after that. c-GER-3013 c-GER-3014

Reported German hedgerow drill: the lead tank fires high explosive, machine guns spray the hedge tops, infantry crosses before the shock wears off. c-GER-3018

Gaps: FM 17-10 is tank-centered; the US tank-infantry pamphlets are not read yet.

individual / sniper / attack

Sniper

key targetsfew shotsoffsetmove often

Thin evidence. Snipers shoot leaders, observers and heavy weapon crews. Stay slightly offset from the squad. Fire three to six rounds from one position, then move. Pair with an observer. In defense, sit at sector limits or open flanks and deny movement.

GERJPSU

How it works, with numbers

German: fleeting high-priority targets: leaders, observers and heavy weapon crews. Soviet: snipers, officers, observers and key weapons, with precise single shots. GER01-0007 SU01-0015

German: work independently inside the mission, slightly offset from the squad to keep fire clear. In an advance go with security elements, and apart from machine gunners. GER01-0008 GER01-0009

Reported of the Germans: in attack stay 10 to 15 yards behind the firing line, on officers and machine gunners. GER03-0170

German: in fortified attacks attach snipers to storm detachments, firing at gun embrasures. GER01-0010

German defense: fire three to six rounds from a position, then change. Pair with an observer with binoculars. Several snipers together deny movement and force observers and weapons under cover. GER01-0012 GER01-0013 GER01-0014

Reported of the Germans: defensive positions at sector limits or open flanks. GER03-0171

Reach. Germans: a sniper must judge range out to 500 m. Soviet: snipers hit targets to 800 m, while ordinary rifle fire does best within 300 m. Use the mod's range in play. GER01-0003 SU01-0182

German: if no target shows, lure fire with a helmet or straw dummy above cover. If the enemy grows too careful, rest the sector for days. c-GER-2001 c-GER-2002

Reported of the Japanese: two snipers per squad, mostly to distract; patient and well hidden, but rarely effective beyond about 50 yards. c-JP-2006

Reported Japanese: a prisoner said each light machine gun squad included a sniper, few with scoped rifles. c-JP-3002

Gaps: German lines: checked second-pass reads, plus lure and rest rules (2026-11-08); the German 400 m figure was not on its page and was dropped. Japanese is reported only. US and UK sniper doctrine not in the digest.

individual / sniper / counter

Snipers and counter-sniping

first careless moveleaders and crewsroofs and towerstempt his fire

Snipers work apart, forward and on the flanks, hunting hidden fire points, leaders and crews. If they miss, they mark targets for MGs and mortars and move. Against them: watch roofs and towers, clear churches early, and find hidden enemies by observation, searching fire and movement that tempts fire.

FINSUUK

How it works, with numbers

Soviet: snipers work apart from the platoon, forward and on the flanks; their first task is finding and killing hidden fire points. c-SU-3021

Reported Finnish views: snipers pick officers, fire directors, automatic riflemen and antitank crews; if they miss, they mark with tracer and move. The duel goes to whoever avoids the first careless move. c-FI-3001 c-FI-3002

UK: covering groups watch the roofs; clear churches early, since towers serve snipers and observers. c-UK-3019 c-UK-3021

UK: find a hidden enemy by observation, searching fire, movement that tempts fire, and snipers. c-UK-3020

Gaps: Finnish views come through a German translation reported by the US. German own sniping doctrine is not sourced.

individual / tank / attack

Tank crew in the attack

target orderhalt to shootkeep movingnever alone

A tank stays within supporting distance of others. It shoots first at enemy tanks able to hurt it, then anti-tank guns, then harmless armor, then troops. Moving fire fails past about 300 yards, so it halts briefly, in cover, to shoot. A halted tank in the open is very vulnerable.

SUUS

How it works, with numbers

A lone tank never operates beyond supporting distance of others. c-USA-0002

Target order: enemy tanks able to hurt ours, then anti-tank guns, then harmless armored vehicles, then personnel and weapons affecting our maneuver. c-USA-0005

Against an anti-tank gun, some tanks fire stationary from hull-down while others close, preferably from flank or rear. c-USA-0006

A halted tank shoots better. Moving fire improves as range closes and generally fails past 300 yards. Advancing tanks change direction and speed to spoil anti-tank fire. c-USA-0008 c-USA-0004

A stationary exposed tank is very vulnerable, so halts show only the turret or stay brief under cover. c-USA-0009

Gaps: Only US doctrine read for tank crews so far. Armor and penetration in the game come from the mod, so the target order is the input, not the outcome.

platoon / at / defense

Anti-tank platoon in defense

split tank from infantrymutual gunsblend incovered mines

Guns, AT rifles and tank hunters fight the tanks while mortars and machine guns strip the infantry. Space guns so a tank overrunning one is flanked by another, inside rifle protection. Don't sit in conspicuous spots. Mines without covering fire barely delay.

GERSUUKUS

How it works, with numbers

Soviet: against tank-infantry attack, AT weapons fight the tanks; mortars, machine guns and submachine guns destroy and separate the infantry. c-SU-0029

US: space guns for mutual support within rifle protection, so a tank overrunning one is flanked by another. c-USI10-0118

Dividing a sector between platoons can leave open tank routes on the boundary. Leaders close them and keep mutual fire, especially while displacing. c-USI10-0072

Site guns by field of fire, observation, cover and concealment, obstacles, and lines in and out. Avoid isolated bushes or debris in the open: pick a background that blends. c-USA02-0063 c-USI02-0130

Dummy works well away from real positions draw fire away from them. Dummy guns should look careless but logical. c-USI10-0121 c-USA02-0071

Mines without covering fire delay only long enough to bypass or lift a passage. Once the enemy expects covered blocks, camouflage alone may halt him under fire. c-USI10-0153 c-USI10-0150

Appearance can mislead, since either side may use captured vehicles. Reconnaissance and decoy vehicles get fire only on a commander's order. c-USI10-0078

Soviet AT rifle platoon: concentrated fire at 300 m, then all rifles at close range on any breakthrough. It can repel medium and light tanks on one tank-danger direction. SU01-0176 SU01-0177 SU01-0160

Reported of the Germans: rocket projector teams spread by squads to protect heavy machine gun positions from armor. GER04-0004

UK: AT guns cover probable tank approaches, in depth and concealed, since the enemy will try to neutralize them by fire or smoke. c-UK-3006

Gaps: UK AT platoon doctrine did not surface in the digest.

  31. c-USI10-0148 US / own A mined road block either extends mines across and beyond the road, or obstructs the road with mines on its flanks preventing detours.

  32. c-USI10-0149 US / own Road block mines need double normal field density; cover surface-laid mines so crews must dismount to inspect them.

  33. c-USI10-0150 US / own Once the enemy expects covered blocks, camouflage material alone, with no mines, may halt his vehicles under the defenders' fire.
    FM 7-35 Infantry: Antitank Company, Infantry Regiment And Antitank Platoon, Infantry Battalion, 1944, leaf 191, p. 178, para 158b(1)
  34. c-USI10-0151 US / own Station men and mines ready at chosen road points, blocking only on order or enemy approach, so friendly traffic runs until the last moment.

  35. c-USI10-0152 US / own A barrier links minefields and road blocks in the gaps between natural or artificial obstacles, making continuous obstruction to armor over large areas.
    FM 7-35 Infantry: Antitank Company, Infantry Regiment And Antitank Platoon, Infantry Battalion, 1944, leaf 191, p. 178, para 159
  36. c-USI10-0153 US / own Mines without covering fire delay the enemy only briefly, just long enough to bypass them or lift a passage.
    FM 7-35 Infantry: Antitank Company, Infantry Regiment And Antitank Platoon, Infantry Battalion, 1944, leaf 192, p. 179, para 160a
  37. c-USI10-0154 US / own Defenders sit in covered, concealed positions overlooking the mined area, stopping removal by fire; antitank guns, when available, finish armor disabled or slowed by mines.

  38. c-USI10-0155 US / own Mines endanger friendly troops too: observers posted during laying become guards who warn and guide through gaps until the covering-fire unit takes over.

  39. c-USI10-0156 US / own When contact is imminent, remove signs or markers that would reveal the mined area, substituting guards if needed.
    FM 7-35 Infantry: Antitank Company, Infantry Regiment And Antitank Platoon, Infantry Battalion, 1944, leaf 194, p. 181, para 161a(2)
  40. c-USI10-0157 US / own Put signs only where friendly approach is likely and hostile unlikely; deceptive signs on dummy areas or passages work if subtle and friendly troops know.
    FM 7-35 Infantry: Antitank Company, Infantry Regiment And Antitank Platoon, Infantry Battalion, 1944, leaf 195, p. 182, para 161b(2)(d)
  41. c-USI10-0158 US / own Fence a forward minefield only behind its rear edge, leaving the front unmarked; isolated inconspicuous markers forward warn friendly patrols.

  42. c-USI10-0159 US / own Fences enclosing minefields run wider than the field with different direction changes, plus crossing wires, so boundaries stay hidden from the enemy.
    FM 7-35 Infantry: Antitank Company, Infantry Regiment And Antitank Platoon, Infantry Battalion, 1944, leaf 196, p. 183, para 161b(3)(d)
  43. c-USI10-0160 US / own Tactical wire before main line may double as mine marking, so wire and mines protect each other; full fencing on outpost or flank betrays mines.

  44. c-USI10-0162 US / own Tanks avoid open ground covered by antitank fire and use concealed corridors; mining those corridors forces them into the open and economizes guns.
    FM 7-35 Infantry: Antitank Company, Infantry Regiment And Antitank Platoon, Infantry Battalion, 1944, leaf 199, p. 186, para 164
  45. c-USI10-0163 US / own With latitude on sites, pick mine locations best coordinated with adjacent obstacles, nearby guns and troops who can cover them with small arms.
    FM 7-35 Infantry: Antitank Company, Infantry Regiment And Antitank Platoon, Infantry Battalion, 1944, leaf 200, p. 187, para 166a
  46. c-USI10-0164 US / own In broken terrain, mine narrow tank approaches to force tanks out of cover into open areas within gun range, ideally exposing their flanks.
    FM 7-35 Infantry: Antitank Company, Infantry Regiment And Antitank Platoon, Infantry Battalion, 1944, leaf 200, p. 187, para 166b
  47. c-USI10-0165 US / own In open terrain, ring the protected area with mines if supply allows; otherwise lay fields canalizing tanks into concentrated antitank fire.
    FM 7-35 Infantry: Antitank Company, Infantry Regiment And Antitank Platoon, Infantry Battalion, 1944, leaf 200, p. 187, para 166b
  48. c-USI10-0176 US / own Battalion platoon mainly gives armor defense to its battalion; all-round security requires coordinating guns with battalion and regimental means, often reinforced by the antitank company.
    FM 7-35 Infantry: Antitank Company, Infantry Regiment And Antitank Platoon, Infantry Battalion, 1944, leaf 211, p. 198, para 178a
  49. c-USI10-0178 US / own Battalion guns are held mobile less often than antitank company guns; readiness otherwise follows the company's practice.
    FM 7-35 Infantry: Antitank Company, Infantry Regiment And Antitank Platoon, Infantry Battalion, 1944, leaf 211, p. 198, para 179
  50. c-USI10-0179 US / own Platoon leader recommends employment in time, blending guns, rifle grenades, rockets, mines and obstacles into one battalion plan, and coordinates with other antitank elements nearby.
    FM 7-35 Infantry: Antitank Company, Infantry Regiment And Antitank Platoon, Infantry Battalion, 1944, leaf 211, p. 198, para 180
  51. c-USI10-0180 US / own As battalion antitank officer, the platoon leader ensures battalion mines have traffic guards and small-arms cover, plus guns, rifle grenades and rockets when possible.
    FM 7-35 Infantry: Antitank Company, Infantry Regiment And Antitank Platoon, Infantry Battalion, 1944, leaf 212, p. 199, para 181b(2)
  52. c-USI10-0190 US / own Bivouacking alone, the platoon usually joins the outpost, covering tank approaches or road blocks; rockets take uncovered approaches; too few guns means holding them mobile.
    FM 7-35 Infantry: Antitank Company, Infantry Regiment And Antitank Platoon, Infantry Battalion, 1944, leaf 218, p. 205, para 185b(2)
  53. c-USI11-0007 US / own Front-line platoon guns, with mines and obstacles, cover the likeliest tank avenues so each tank is engaged before reaching the main line of resistance.
    FM 7-35 Infantry: Antitank Company, Infantry Regiment And Antitank Platoon, Infantry Battalion, 1944, leaf 236, p. 223, para 207a
  54. c-USI11-0008 US / own Site guns near the first terrain feature behind the line if they can fire ahead of it; otherwise inside forward platoon areas. Prefer flanking fire.
    FM 7-35 Infantry: Antitank Company, Infantry Regiment And Antitank Platoon, Infantry Battalion, 1944, leaf 236, p. 223, para 207a
  55. c-USI11-0009 US / own Guns are mutually supporting, so a tank overrunning one position is hit in flank by another; regimental company guns add depth.
    FM 7-35 Infantry: Antitank Company, Infantry Regiment And Antitank Platoon, Infantry Battalion, 1944, leaf 236, p. 223, para 207a
  56. c-USI11-0010 US / own On the general outpost the platoon covers roads and tank avenues; if holding for a set time it organizes firing positions, prime movers close by.
    FM 7-35 Infantry: Antitank Company, Infantry Regiment And Antitank Platoon, Infantry Battalion, 1944, leaf 237, p. 224, para 207b
  57. c-USI11-0012 US / own Reserve battalion platoon guards the assembly area; in position it limits tank penetration, protects flanks and rear, and supplements forward guns if fields allow.
    FM 7-35 Infantry: Antitank Company, Infantry Regiment And Antitank Platoon, Infantry Battalion, 1944, leaf 237, p. 224, para 207d
  58. c-USI11-0013 US / own Fire plan overlay fixes each gun's sector, principal direction, primary, supplementary and alternate positions, opening conditions, and which guns engage reconnaissance or decoy vehicles.
    FM 7-35 Infantry: Antitank Company, Infantry Regiment And Antitank Platoon, Infantry Battalion, 1944, leaf 238, p. 225, para 208b
  59. c-USI11-0014 US / own Supplementary positions must lie close enough to primary firing positions that guns can be moved between them by hand.
    FM 7-35 Infantry: Antitank Company, Infantry Regiment And Antitank Platoon, Infantry Battalion, 1944, leaf 238, p. 225, para 209a
  60. c-USI11-0053 US / own Front-line platoons keep ammunition at each emplacement; platoons held mobile keep it on vehicles. Rocket launcher emplacements give firing positions close-in protection.
    FM 7-35 Infantry: Antitank Company, Infantry Regiment And Antitank Platoon, Infantry Battalion, 1944, leaf 299, p. unknown, para App. IV 5g

  62. c-USI11-0055 US / own Platoon leaders name terrain features armor must pass before guns open; only guns designated in the company order fire at apparent reconnaissance vehicles.

  63. c-USI11-0056 US / own Remaining guns hold fire until the tank attack is definitely committed and within effective range.
    FM 7-35 Infantry: Antitank Company, Infantry Regiment And Antitank Platoon, Infantry Battalion, 1944, leaf 303, p. 290, para App. IV 5i
  64. c-USI11-0058 US / own Adjacent rifle units secure guns against foot troops; when attacked, men not operating the gun fight from fox holes with individual weapons.

    FM 18-20 Tank Destroyer, Tactical Employment Of Tank Destroyer Platoon, Self-propelled 1944, leaf 23, p. 19, para 14a

    FM 18-20 Tank Destroyer, Tactical Employment Of Tank Destroyer Platoon, Self-propelled 1944, leaf 32, p. 28, para 25

    FM 18-20 Tank Destroyer, Tactical Employment Of Tank Destroyer Platoon, Self-propelled 1944, leaf 56, p. 52, para 43b

platoon / infantry / attack

Platoon attack

fire and movementflankcovered approachone squad back

Frontal fire pins the enemy while others maneuver, and the roles may swap. Keep one squad back at first unless every rifle is needed. Choose a covered approach that isn't the obvious one, and keep attacking the first post even when its neighbors open up.

GERITJPSUUKUS

How it works, with numbers

Once effective fire arrives, the platoon moves by fire and movement: one part pins, the rest maneuver. When one element draws fire, the others keep going and help from the enemy's flank. c-US-1060 c-US-1052

Keep one rifle squad back at first as a maneuver element, then send it at the least-resisted point or round a flank. c-US-1056 c-US-1061

Supporting fire should be oblique: fired frontally for a flank attack, or from a flank for a frontal one. c-UK-1033

Pick a covered approach the enemy hasn't already covered, since he read the ground too. Avoid a wide encircling move into open ground, where it draws enfilade fire. c-UK-1035 c-UK-1042

British battle drill: the scout section tries alone; if it fails it becomes the fire section holding fire superiority. c-UK-1034

The post is probably part of a supporting system, and its neighbors may hold fire until the flanking move starts. Keep attacking the first post, detaching as little as possible. Fighting every post breaks the platoon up. c-UK-1036 c-UK-1037 c-UK-1038

Heavy flank fire: flankers drop to cover, a gun group answers, the rest push on. Mortar smoke can serve as artificial cover. c-UK-1039 c-UK-1040

Don't attack straight off the march unless forced, as reconnaissance and coordination get little chance. Scouts should keep the platoon secure from fire inside midrange, given as 400 to 600 yards. c-US-1055 c-US-1054

If flanking is impossible, infiltrate a small assaulting party in close, covered by the remaining fire. Thin cover can often hide a few riflemen, not more. c-US-1062 c-US-1057

Reported of the Germans: a platoon attacks on 165 to 220 yards. c-GER-0010

Soviet: a platoon attacks on up to 150 meters, with firing lines 150 to 250 apart, and the reserve platoon follows 200 to 300 behind. A leader who finds a gap or a suppressed weapon pushes through, even off direction, to reach flank and rear. c-SU-0015 c-SU-0016 c-SU-0020 c-SU-0018

Gaps: US squad and platoon pamphlets are not read yet; this rests on FM 7-10 and British Part VIII. Soviet is in mediocre OCR.

platoon / infantry / defense

Platoon defense

no unswept groundhold firealternate firstthrow them out

Leave no unswept ground within 400 m of the forward edge, and hide the weapons. Fire first from alternate positions, or hold for surprise, and take primary positions at 300 m. Enemy who enter are thrown out by fire or counterattack. Frontage is 200 to 500 yards.

GERJPSUUKUS

How it works, with numbers

Frontage: US 200 to 400 yards with protected flanks, depth at most 200 yards. Soviet up to 500 m wide and 250 m deep with reinforcements and neighbours. c-USI12-0124 c-USI12-0123 c-SU-0025

Reported of the Germans: normal sector 220 to 550 yards. c-GER-0030

Soviet fire plan: no unswept ground within 400 m of the forward edge, with weapons hidden from observation. c-SU-0026

Soviet: weapons first fire from alternate positions and take primary ones at 300 m. A concealed platoon may instead hold fire until then for surprise. c-SU-0028

Each US section group covers its own and its neighbours' fronts and flanks, on about 200 yards. c-USI06-0007

Enemy who get into the position are thrown out by fire or counterattack. Hold fire until the attacker is close. c-USI05-0064

Soviet: stay under cover through shelling and move up to pre-designated positions when it stops. Hit a penetration with fire from flank and rear. SU01-0127 SU01-0128

Soviet digging order: within an hour, clear fields of fire and dig standing trenches; within four to five hours, add slits and light obstacles on threatened approaches. SU04-0104 SU04-0105

Soviet: a reinforced platoon as battalion combat outpost stands 1 to 2 km ahead of the forward edge. c-SU-0032

UK: site a post from the enemy side: his likeliest approach, the part vital to the defence, and how to counter-attack it if lost. c-UK-3004

Gaps: UK platoon defense rests on one siting line from Part VIII; its work tables are left out.

platoon / infantry / town

Clearing a village

back gardenstop downfire sectionkilling ground

A fire section suppresses the main street; clearing sections alternate through the houses, entering from the back, top floor downward. Don't encircle: an escape route onto a killing ground beats desperate defenders. Thin evidence, nearly all from one UK manual.

GERSUUKUS

How it works, with numbers

UK: leading troops bypass towns and following units clear them systematically. UK01-0113

UK: clear from back gardens and yards, which gives covered approaches and catches escapers with street fire. The ideal is to enter at the top and clear downward, forcing defenders into worse positions, though the source admits this is often not possible. UK01-0114 UK01-0115

UK: assault sections alternate clearing and covering. A third section suppresses windows and openings on the main street from the rear, moving up as the clearing sections advance. UK01-0140 UK01-0147

UK: if one section is fixed, the other keeps going. UK01-0142

UK: encircled enemies fight harder, so provide a killing ground on the main line of retreat outside the village. An ambush party gets there covertly before clearing begins. UK01-0146 UK01-0144

UK: a following platoon passes through once a space is clear, keeping the offensive going. UK05-0067

US: attach guns, machine guns and light mortars to the rifle platoon in a town; howitzers and heavier mortars stay under company control. c-USI17-0187

Reported of the Germans: in a town the main line runs well inside the built-up area, irregular for flanking fire, because the edges make easy artillery targets. c-GER-0045

Soviet: a town strongpoint garrison is a reinforced platoon with large reserves of food and ammunition. SU02-0055

Soviet: hold a town with minimum infantry and a strong mobile reserve. Each strongpoint holds all round: a small building a squad or platoon, a large one a company. c-SU-2033 c-SU-2035

Soviet: successive lines of strongpoints in mutual support, enfilading streets; artillery centralised outside the town, decentralised inside. c-SU-2034 c-SU-2037

Soviet: defend actively with ambushes and point-blank fire through holes in walls; clear fields of fire and block unused windows. c-SU-2036 c-SU-2038

Soviet: tanks wait in weakened wooden buildings to burst out; barricades, AT mines and booby traps sit under enfilade fire. c-SU-2039 c-SU-2040

Reported German town attack: flank and encircle; if assaulting, mass all fire on the forward edge and isolated houses, infantry going in as fire lifts. c-GER-3002

UK village clearing: platoon HQ stays with the fire section guarding its rear; the commander coordinates, not leading one section. c-UK-3003

Soviet: attack a town frontally with part of the force, main blow toward its rear; defend it from the heights outside, with strong crossroads buildings flanking each other. c-SU-3019 c-SU-3020

Gaps: UK lines are checked reads of one manual; Soviet town defense read from BUP-2. German street fighting is reported, not German own text.

platoon / recon / recon

Reconnaissance platoon

pairssee not fightbypass and reportverify

Never send a lone vehicle: work in pairs. Prioritize observation over fighting, bypass superior force and report it. Move fast on roads far off, cover to cover when near. To find a well-trained enemy, one element covers while another dashes out and draws fire.

GERSUUKUS

How it works, with numbers

Operate in sections or groups of at least two vehicles, because lone vehicles get ambushed. A platoon thus covers only two roads and the ground between. c-USA01-0186

US: usually one section per route; a zone at most 2 miles wide. Soviet: up to 12 km beyond the security line by day, 3 km at night. c-USA03-0062 c-USA03-0063 c-SU-0014

Soviet: observation before combat, fighting only to break through, take prisoners or avoid destruction. Secretly bypass superior force and report it at once. SU04-0149 SU05-0001

Soviet: fast on roads when far off, bounds from cover to cover when near. When necessary, ambush at point-blank range. SU04-0147 SU05-0002

US, drawing fire: one element covers the locality while another approaches slowly, then suddenly dashes off firing back. c-USA03-0073

If a block can be bypassed, report its exact location and preferably leave a two-vehicle section watching it. c-USA02-0018

After contact, locate and hold hostile flanks, and check routes, crossings and critical areas for ambushes, blocks and mines. Hold contact until the enemy outruns you or main forces engage. c-USI08-0095 c-USI08-0114

Never accept stragglers' reports unverified, even when several agree. c-USA03-0079

Reported German: recon advances by bounds, shorter near the enemy, with different routes out and back; raiding patrols of 15 to 20 seek prisoners. c-GER-3004 c-GER-3005

Gaps: UK and German recon platoon doctrine barely surfaced. The bot equivalent is sparse: decide scouting by role availability in the game.

squad / infantry / assault

Section assault and consolidation

gun coversflank positiongo pastdig in

The gun group fires until the rifle group crosses the post, then covers consolidation. The rifle group attacks from the flank, about 3 o'clock to the post, goes through without stopping and reorganizes at least 50 yards beyond it, because the captured post draws mortar fire.

GERSUUKUS

How it works, with numbers

British battle drill. In the advance the gun group stays at the rear, so effective fire is less likely to stop the whole section. After the first reaction, fire opens only on definite orders. c-UK-1053 c-UK-1054

The rifle group moves off so it doesn't assault from where it fired. In the right flanking drill the assault position is 3 o'clock to the post, with the gun group covering from 10 or 2 o'clock. c-UK-1055 c-UK-1056

On the commander's order the rifle group assaults firing from the hip. The gun group fires rapid and stops when the group crosses the post. c-UK-1057 c-UK-1060

Without halting, the group wheels back to its original line and consolidates at least 50 yards past the post. c-UK-1058

Don't linger around the post, which draws mortar fire. If staying, dig in at once. c-UK-1059

Clear the whole objective, as small detachments can revive after the first shock. c-UK-1052

US company doctrine sets the same aim higher up: drive through the depth to the final objective and exploit at once. c-US-1044

Soviet: the squad stays close behind its own bursts, since lagging raises losses. Fire opens in stages while closing: light machine gun at 600 meters, best shots at 400, all rifles at 300. It breaks in from 40 to 50 meters. c-SU-0005 c-SU-0003 c-SU-0006

Gaps: Mostly one British source (Part VIII, 1944). The US rifle squad manual is not read yet. The source prints one clock value wrongly, so 2 o'clock is a correction.

squad / infantry / attack

Squad attack

staged fireshort rushesfire slackens gogap rush

Open fire in stages while closing: light machine gun far out, best shots next, all rifles last. Any slackening of enemy fire is the order to advance. Nations disagree on open ground: short fast rushes, or longer bounds under overwhelming fire.

JPSUUKUS

How it works, with numbers

Soviet fire stages: light machine gun from 600 m, best shots from 400 m, all riflemen from 300 m. c-SU-0003

US: the squad holds fire until 500 yards. In good conditions the automatic rifle engages from 500 to 1,000 yards, like a light machine gun. Short bursts on frontal fire, longer ones on compact or enfiladed targets. c-USI02-0008 c-USI02-0028

Rushes differ. Soviet: the more open the ground and the heavier the fire, the shorter and faster the rush. US: a short rush from cover into open ground only adds losses; very open ground needs overwhelming fire and longer bounds. c-SU-0002 c-USI04-0153

Soviet: any slackening of enemy fire or growth of your own is an order to advance at once. c-SU-0004

Soviet: a squad spotting a weak point rushes it, even off direction, then strikes flank and rear. c-SU-0007

Soviet submachine gun squads: effective only to 200 m, so close stealthily, open with sudden massed fire, and use gaps to reach crew weapons and headquarters from flank or rear. SU01-0032 SU01-0033

UK: two Brens at very short range give close support over the final yards of the assault. UK01-0027

US: skirmishers at five-pace intervals cover about 60 paces. Don't let men bunch behind one-man cover or use isolated, well-defined objects. c-USI03-0007 c-USI04-0160

Reported of the Japanese: final deployment comes in time to fire during the last few hundred yards before the assault. JP03-0018

Gaps: The rush-length disagreement is real doctrine, not resolved here. Treat it as national flavor, or tune it in play.

squad / infantry / tank-hunting

Close-range tank hunting

stop it firstlead tank firstblind sidepicked menkill the following infantry

Stop the tank first with mines or obstacles, then close in from its blind side and finish it with grenades, charges or flame on the vision slits or engine deck. Hit the lead tank first. Hunters are picked men, often one team per platoon. The rest of the infantry kills the infantry following the tanks.

JPSUUKUS

How it works, with numbers

US: mines stop tanks by the running gear, then incendiary or antitank grenades finish them. c-US-3002

Soviet: knock out the lead tank first; the flamethrower aims at vision slits or the rear engine deck. c-SU-3005

UK: tank-hunting parties are picked men, ideally one platoon. Forward infantry’s main task is stopping the infantry that follow, leaving tanks to anti-tank weapons. c-UK-3010 c-UK-3011

Reported Japanese practice: hunter teams, perhaps one per platoon, attack weak points or raid tank parks; tanks halted in towns by obstacles become their targets. c-JP-3006 c-JP-3007

Soviet: the anti-tank rifle section fights counterattacking tanks and, in towns, dug-in tanks and fire points in houses. c-SU-3008

Gaps: German own close anti-tank drill is not in this pass. In game, close assault is a grenade or charge thrown by a nearby unit; reach and effect are per mod.

Evidence: 7 claims
  1. c-US-3002 US / own Mines stop tanks by their running gear; incendiary or antitank grenades then finish them. In an ambush, mines block the lead and rear tanks.
    Fm18-5, leaf 128
  2. c-UK-3010 UK / own By day, reserve or mobile infantry ambush small tank groups; tank-hunting parties are specially picked men, ideally formed as one platoon.
    Infantry Training, Part VIII. – Fieldcraft, Battle Drill, Section and Platoon Tactics, leaf 129
  3. c-UK-3011 UK / own Against tanks, forward infantry’s main task is stopping the infantry that follow; anti-tank weapons and reserve tanks deal with the tanks.
    Infantry Training, Part VIII. – Fieldcraft, Battle Drill, Section and Platoon Tactics, leaf 128
  4. c-JP-3006 JP / reported Reported of the Japanese: tank-hunting teams, perhaps one per platoon, attack vulnerable points or raid tank parks.
    Untitled source 3, leaf 186
  5. c-JP-3007 JP / reported Reported of the Japanese: tanks halted in towns by obstacles and fire become targets for tank hunters.
    Untitled source 3, leaf 222
  6. c-SU-3005 SU / own Knock out the lead tank first. The flamethrower aims at vision slits or the rear engine deck.
    Боевой устав пехоты Красной Армии. Ч. 1. (Боец, отделение, взвод, рота), leaf 29, p. 26
  7. c-SU-3008 SU / own The anti-tank rifle section suppresses pillboxes and fights counterattacking tanks; in towns it engages dug-in tanks and fire points in houses and cellars.
    Боевой устав пехоты Красной Армии. Ч. 1. (Боец, отделение, взвод, рота), leaf 78, p. 75

In the game: rules

Rules name roles and ratios, never unit names or metres, so one rule holds on any mod. A fit tag says how far the game can express it: direct the game has it, proxy only approximately, engine depends on the adaptation, out skip it.

force policy

Own the shape your size can run

When A bot buys or re-plans, and its squads on hand are known

  • Up to 6 squads: one base of fire and one maneuver element, keeping a squad back at first if there are enough. Don't split further.
  • 7 to 15: support group, two maneuver groups, a small reserve.
  • 16 to 28: support group, company-size groups, a real reserve.
  • Change shape at a phase change, never during an assault.

Every echelon read here uses the same form: something fires, something moves, something stays back. Spreading too thin costs control.

shape enginethresholds engine

force policy

Never buy one arm alone

When Choosing the next purchases

  • Have a base of fire (mg) before adding more maneuver squads.
  • Have anti-tank means before the enemy can field armor, and more once it does.
  • Buy tanks with supporting infantry and fire, not as a tank-only force.
  • A tank alone doesn't count as a group: keep tanks in twos or more.

Tanks are not self-sufficient, and massed tanks fail against a working anti-tank screen without other arms (the second is reported of the Germans).

role order enginegroup of tanks engine

force policy

Answer armor by massing, scaled to what was seen

When Enemy armor is seen, or could arrive and its strength is unknown

  • Strength unknown: hold anti-tank means massed, in one place you can move.
  • Small-scale armor only: spread light anti-tank among forward groups.
  • Fewer anti-tank weapons on hand means a larger share massed.

US tank destroyer doctrine sets distribution by the armor threat, with concentration first.

seen armor trigger enginebuying engine

force policy

Keep something uncommitted

When Any purchase or commitment while a fight is on

  • Treat unspent income as part of the reserve: keep enough for one group's worth of answers (design).
  • Spend it at once for a decisive blow, a counterattack, or to restart a stalled attack.
  • After spending, rebuild a reserve from relieved units before attacking again.

US and British manuals both keep a support back and insist on rebuilding it. Money as reserve is the pack author's own translation, since a match can buy where a real company couldn't.

money as reserve proxytiming engine

tactical policy

One main effort, on the best-covered ground

When Team or bot is choosing where to attack

  • Score axes by cover on the way in and by enemy strength; pick one.
  • Team: one bot or pair is main effort, the others hold or fix.
  • Bot: most maneuver groups on that axis; the rest press to split the enemy.
  • If a unit isn't stopped, it keeps going while neighbors are halted.

An even advance is unlikely to succeed. Positions are unevenly held, and covered approaches reach their weak spots.

axis choice enginecover score proxyteam coordination engine

tactical policy

Attack narrow, defend at double, delay at double again

When Assigning a group a width on the map

  • Attack width W: 1.0 x mg per company-shape bot, 0.5 x mg per platoon-shape bot (design).
  • Defense width 2 x W, delay width 4 x W. A bot only fixing or holding uses 2 x W.
  • Widen by gaps between groups covered by fire, not by thinning a group.
  • Too narrow also fails: bunching raises losses.

US figures (200-500 yd attack, 500-1,000 defense, double again in delay) and the reported German rule give the same 1:2:4. The ratio survives a mod's range change; yards don't.

frontage engine

tactical policy

Something fires while something moves

When Group in contact, or moving where the enemy can fire

  • Split: base of fire pins, maneuver moves. They may swap.
  • Site the base to fire obliquely, about 0.6 to 0.8 x mg from the objective (design).
  • Maneuver goes by a covered route that isn't the obvious one, never a wide loop in the open.
  • Keep on the first post; detach the least possible to answer flank fire.

Every move is covered by fire at every echelon read. Fighting every post breaks the unit up.

base and maneuver enginepin effect proxyroute choice engine

tactical policy

Lift late, shift guns to the flanks

When Maneuver group is near the objective

  • Close to the nearest point that doesn't mask supporting fire, then assault.
  • Before that, move guns toward the flank of the resistance, so they fire longest.
  • When masked, mg and mortars shift to enemy beside or behind the objective.
  • Assault together. A piecemeal assault loses much of its effect.

The same sequence appears in US infantry, US tank and British drill.

timing enginefire shift proxy

tactical policy

Keep a support, spend it whole, rebuild it

When A group is held back, or an attack stalls

  • Exposed flank or unclear enemy: hold back more, up to two of three groups.
  • Hold while fires or other groups can restart the attack.
  • Commit whole, at once, at a flank or at weakness; never reinforce strong resistance.
  • Then rebuild one from relieved or stray units.

Holding back is what lets a commander shape the later fight, and only quick use denies the enemy repair time.

holding enginecommit trigger engine

tactical policy

Go past the objective, then dig in

When A group has just taken an objective

  • Don't stop on it: move a short way past (design 0.1 to 0.2 x rifle).
  • Bring mg and light AT up at once to cover front and open flanks.
  • If not advancing, set all-round defense and enter cover.
  • Clear the whole objective.

A captured post draws mortar fire, and infantry is most exposed to tanks while reorganizing.

move past enginetake cover directweapons forward engine

tactical policy

Forward positions that cover each other

When Force is on the defensive or holding what it took

  • Two parts forward, one back; each covers its neighbor.
  • Block covered approaches with troops; cover open ground with mg fire.
  • Depth between positions: within rifle range of each other (design 0.5 to 1.0 x rifle).
  • Riflemen hold fire to effective range, heavy weapons open earlier.
  • Prefer reverse slopes where the map offers them.

US doctrine, with the reverse slope reported of the Germans.

layout enginehold fire engineentrench direct

tactical policy

Hit the flank before he organizes

When A held point has just fallen and a reserve exists

  • Go at once, whole, at the flank of the penetration.
  • Fire across its base to stop more entering.
  • Stop at the old line. Beyond it, fire only.
  • Enemy armor seen near and able to reach it: keep the reserve, hold a flank line, and use tac.at-screen.

Must land before the enemy reorganizes. US doctrine, also reported of the Germans.

trigger engineflank choice enginestop line engine

tactical policy

Leave early, covering in turn

When A group can't hold and has somewhere to go

  • Go before the enemy is within 0.5 x rifle or rifle fire is hurting you.
  • One part covers while the rest moves, then swap. Last out has a covered route.
  • Delay: spread wide, fire from maximum range, then go when he deploys.
  • Successive lines no farther apart than 1.0 x mg, so each covers the last.
  • The withdrawal is an order in both mods. Auto-move only: vanilla idle soldiers may also fall back alone, so expect leaks; the overhaul mod's idle soldiers never do (no_retreat).

Daylight withdrawal under fire is costly; the manuals insist on leaving before contact pins troops.

order enginevanilla auto retreat direct

tactical policy

Hide, wait, shoot from the flank

When Enemy armor is possible on a route

  • Be in place before tanks arrive. Stay hidden.
  • Site for flank shots; platoons cover each other's dead ground.
  • Hold fire inside gun range (design 0.6 x gun_medium, or vision if shorter). Others stay silent until enemy tanks turn toward the first gun.
  • Save AT ammunition for armor. Never chase.
  • Keep infantry next to the guns; don't call terrain impassable.

US destroyer doctrine and reported German practice both use concealment, flanking fire and very late opening.

placement enginehold fire engineconcealment proxy

tactical policy

Tanks envelop; infantry first if obstacles

When A group with tanks attacks

  • Default: support fires frontally, tanks go under cover to a flank.
  • Known AT obstacles or fortifications: infantry first, tanks fire from behind.
  • When tanks lead, infantry follows at once, in small groups clear of the tanks.
  • Assault only once AT weapons are gone; all together.
  • Stalled: fall back to a rally point and retry.

US and British agree on exploiting at once. The German order is reported, not first-hand.

sequence enginefollow distance enginerally engine

tactical policy

Tank target order and halts

When A tank has targets, or is about to fire on the move

  • Order: enemy tanks that can hurt it, AT guns, harmless armor, troops.
  • Against an AT gun: some fire from cover, others close from a flank.
  • Halt briefly, in cover, to shoot; beyond short range don't fire on the move for effect.
  • Stay within support of another tank.

US tank doctrine. 'Can hurt it' should come from the mod's own penetration data, not a table here.

target priority proxyhull down enginepairing engine

tactical policy

Mortars for small, known targets

When Mortars are available and ammunition is finite

  • Fire at located guns or men, clearly stopping the advance, and on counterattacks.
  • Never search woods, crests, big building groups or unknown areas.
  • Keep them under central control, near the front.
  • Save some for reserves that exploit without a fire plan.

Ammunition was the limit in both US and British manuals. Check it against each mod's ammo.

target choice proxyammo care engine

tactical policy

Smoke on the enemy, timed to the move

When A group must cross ground an enemy weapon watches, or an unseen weapon fires

  • Located target in range: HE. Unlocated or out of range: smoke on it or its field of view.
  • Smoke the enemy weapon, never a curtain in front of own units.
  • Start just before the move, keep it up until cover: rounds = (gap / speed) / profile smoke life (vanilla about 60 s, the overhaul mod's grenade about 90 s).
  • Skip if it blinds own overwatch or a neighbour's lane. Wind moves no smoke in game, so doctrine wind rules drop out.
  • Enemy smoke: laid weapons keep firing on approaches; reserve moves up.

US tests: smoke on the enemy gave a four-to-one fire advantage. Smoke was about 20 percent of mortar shell, so it went to the decisive move.

smoke round directsmoke decision enginewind outround life direct

tactical policy

Bait to find him, hold fire against his bait

When Enemy weapons unknown, or the enemy shows a lone or easy target

  • A cheap element shows itself or fires; hidden killers are laid where a reply would come from and hit it at once.
  • Only units named for it engage scouts and lone vehicles; AT guns hold to the set range.
  • Feint on a second axis; if it finds weakness it becomes the main effort.
  • Withdrawing: a few weapons keep firing to mimic the position.
  • Ambush in close ground or defiles: open close, keep a way out, never chase.

US doctrine expects feints and decoys to draw early AT fire and names the guns that may answer. The Japanese were reported to bait heavy weapons with LMG fire for their mortars.

probe and kill enginehold fire proxyfeint engineambush proxydummies out

tactical policy

Hold behind the crest when the forward slope is watched

When Defending a ridge or rise the enemy can see from his side, or under enemy artillery or long-range tank fire

  • Main position just behind the crest, out of sight of enemy units beyond close range; weapons laid on the crest line.
  • One or two outposts on the forward slope or crest to see and warn; they fall back on contact.
  • Most of the force held back as a counterattack group aimed at the crest.
  • If the crest is lost, counterattack it at once: whoever holds it sees the whole position.
  • Woods count as a reverse slope; sit back from the wood edge, not on it.

US, UK, Soviet and reported German doctrine agree: the forward slope is untenable under observed fire; the crest becomes a killing ground the enemy must cross in view.

siting enginecrest from heightmap engineoutpost fallback proxycounterattack engine

tactical policy

Ambush in close ground, open on the main body, leave fast

When Own force is weaker or holding, and the enemy must pass through close ground (woods, town, defile, hedges)

  • Two or more parties on both sides of the route, staggered so their fire does not cross into each other.
  • Hold fire until the main body is in close range; let the scouts through.
  • One unit opens the ambush, all fire at once; first targets are leaders, AT crews and vehicles stopped by mines.
  • Against tanks: mine or block the lead and rear vehicles first.
  • Strike, then leave by a planned covered route before the enemy can reply in strength; never chase.

Soviet, British and reported Japanese practice: surprise at close range decides; British drill lets scouts pass and opens on the leader's signal.

hold fire proxyopen together enginemines directexit engine

tactical policy

Pass small groups through unwatched ground; counter with all-round posts

When Attack: a route the enemy does not watch exists past his line. Defense: enemy infantry appears behind or between posts

  • Attack: send a small, well-armed group (SMG, MG, light mortar) along the unwatched route while the main attack holds the front.
  • Its targets are the enemy's rear: heavy weapons, AT guns, crews, and the line the main attack must cross.
  • Defense: every post can fire all round; do not pull posts back when infiltrators appear.
  • Use the reserve to hunt the infiltrators, pivoting on the posts.

Reported German and Soviet practice used infiltration under darkness, fog or rough ground to save losses; US doctrine set all-round posts and aggressive reserves as the answer.

route finding engineall round proxyhunt engine

tactical policy

Stop the tank, close from the blind side, kill its infantry first

When Enemy tanks within close range of own infantry with grenades, charges, AT rifles or flame

  • Most infantry fire on the infantry with or behind the tanks; separated tanks are far easier to kill.
  • Named hunter teams, about one per platoon, close in from the rear or flank where the tank cannot see.
  • Strike the lead tank first; tanks stopped by mines, obstacles or town streets are first targets.
  • Do not send hunters across open ground in the tank's view.

UK: forward infantry's job is the following infantry, tanks go to AT weapons and hunters. Soviet: lead tank first. US: mines stop it, grenades finish it.

close assault directblind side approach enginetarget split engine

tactical policy

Hold the embrasures, blind it, cut a lane, close from the flank

When A bunker, pillbox, emplaced gun or fortified building blocks the advance

  • Find it: embrasures, and where it can flank the approach.
  • Guns, tanks or MGs fire on the embrasures from a flank; smoke blinds the rest.
  • Engineers clear wire or mines; the assault party closes from the side the embrasures don't cover, with flame or charges.
  • Other units bypass it and watch its exits; once it is silent, the attack continues at once.

Soviet and reported German drills agree on embrasure fire, smoke, lane and close assault. US: tank destroyers can reduce bunkers.

embrasure fire directsmoke directflame directbreach proxybypass engine

tactical policy

Assault guns at the main effort, tank destroyers kept out of close combat

When Force has assault guns or tank destroyers

  • Assault guns go with the infantry of the main effort, firing HE on the points that hold it up.
  • Tank destroyers wait in overwatch for tanks, away from close enemy infantry, with their own infantry or MG cover.
  • Either can fire on bunkers once enemy AT is suppressed.

Reported German use put assault guns at the main effort; US doctrine kept tank destroyers out of close combat and gave them their own security.

role from unit data directplacement engine

tactical policy

Pursue at once, broad and fast, to a set limit

When Enemy units are falling back, or his force ratio drops sharply in a sector

  • Go at once with the nearest fast units; don't wait for neighbours.
  • Press on a broad front against his flanks; send groups by the shortest routes to cut his retreat.
  • Bring MGs, mortars and guns forward so he can't re-form.
  • Bypass strongpoints and rearguards; stop at a set limit (his next prepared line or own support range) and consolidate.

Soviet doctrine makes pursuit relentless but bounded: reserve counterattacks pursue to a set depth.

trigger enginepursue limit enginebypass engine

tactical policy

Snipers hunt hidden weapons and leaders; watch roofs and tempt fire

When Own or enemy snipers present, or a hidden weapon is firing

  • Own sniper: forward or on a flank, apart from the platoon; first targets are MG crews, AT crews, officers and spotters.
  • Move after firing or after a miss; mark targets for MGs and mortars.
  • Against enemy snipers: watch roofs, towers and steeples; clear them early.
  • Find a hidden enemy with searching fire or a cheap unit moving to tempt a shot, then answer with HE.

Soviet, UK and reported Finnish doctrine: snipers hunt fire points and leaders; the duel goes to whoever makes the first careless move.

target priority enginerelocate enginebait engine

tactical policy

Machine guns in enfilade, crossing fire, no gap at the flanks

When Any defense with machine guns

  • Site MGs on the flanks of the position, firing across the front, not straight ahead.
  • Neighbouring MGs' fields cross; check each flank is covered.
  • Heavy MGs take the long fixed lines; light MGs fill the gaps near posts.

UK and US doctrine: the MG is the strongest defensive weapon, best in enfilade on crossing fixed lines.

siting enginefixed lines proxy

terrain-and-special policy

Move concealed, spread on open ground, bound by terrain

When A group is moving and contact is not yet made

  • Use covered routes first, in column while cover lasts.
  • Open ground: spread groups to about 1.5 x rifle apart (design).
  • Stop at terrain bounds; the next group moves only once this bound is secure.
  • Air or tank warning: leave the road for the nearest cover, disperse.

Concealed arrival keeps the force whole and hides its axis until deployment.

routes enginespacing proxybounds engine

terrain-and-special policy

Scout in pairs, observe, report, don't brawl

When Enemy positions are unknown or an axis is being chosen

  • Send at least two elements together, never one alone.
  • One covers while the other moves up, then dashes back to draw fire and reveal guns.
  • Superior force: don't fight; bypass, mark it, and keep one element watching.
  • Feed what is found to axis choice and to the AT and mortar target lists.
  • Fight only to break through or to avoid destruction.

Lone scouts get ambushed, and a scout in a brawl stops telling you anything.

pairing proxycontact report enginedraw fire engine

terrain-and-special policy

Fire down the street, clear from the back, leave a way out

When Objective is a built-up area

  • Bypass with leading groups if possible; a following group clears.
  • Fire element suppresses street-facing windows; assault elements enter from the rear.
  • Assault sections alternate clearing and covering; fire element moves up in bounds.
  • Don't encircle: leave one retreat line and cover it with a fire element or tanks.
  • Defending: hold inside the built-up area, not on its edge.

Rear approaches are covered and catch escapers, and cornered defenders fight harder.

enter buildings enginestreet fire proxyexit lane engine

terrain-and-special policy

Don't linger on an edge; reserve close

When Route or objective lies in woods

  • Cross open ground to the near edge under smoke or concealment if possible.
  • Halt briefly inside the edge, not on it, to restore contact.
  • Keep the reserve within about 1 x rifle of the lead.
  • Stop short of the far edge, then leave in one rush if shelled, or filter out if under small-arms fire.
  • Soviet habit worth copying: bypass a strong woodland point and let followers kill it.

Edges draw artillery. Short sight lines break control, so distances must shrink.

edge avoidance enginegroup cohesion proxymortar clearance out

terrain-and-special policy

Night or low vision means straight ahead and simple

When Mission or weather shortens vision

  • Keep groups in column and deploy only close to the objective.
  • No envelopment: one direct assault on a point already scouted.
  • Narrow each weapon's sector and raise density on the line.
  • A group that stops loses its order: set all-round defense where it stands.
  • Patrol the gaps between held points.

Combined moves in the dark produce confused assaults and friendly fire.

vision trigger proxysector narrowing proxysilence out

terrain-and-special policy

Crossings are chokes; several points, then rally

When A river, bridge or ford lies on the axis

  • Cover the far bank with fire before anything crosses.
  • Cross at more than one point when the map allows.
  • Infantry first, abreast; heavy weapons and vehicles after the far bank holds.
  • Rally on the first prominent feature; don't stop on the bank.
  • Lead elements take an undefended crossing at once rather than waiting.

A crossing bunches troops under observed fire, and the bank is the worst place to halt.

crossing choice engineboats outfar bank cover proxy

terrain-and-special policy

Snipers hunt key men and keep moving

When A sniper unit is available

  • Target order: gun and mortar crews, MG crews, commanders, then enemy snipers.
  • Site offset from the squad, at sector limits or open flanks.
  • Fire a few rounds, then change position.
  • Attack: stay just behind the firing line, with the security element.

A single shot on a crew removes a weapon. Staying put gets the sniper found.

target priority directrelocation engineoffset proxy

terrain-and-special policy

Off-map or heavy fire goes at guns and observers, not at everything

When Heavy guns or fire support are available

  • Targets, in order: AT guns, observation posts, enemy guns, front-line positions.
  • Keep impact a clear margin from own troops; lift when the assault closes.
  • Don't spend it on what tanks or mortars reach faster, or on clearing mines.
  • Sudden short fire, then move; no long preparation.

Long preparations don't fit a match, and support is only useful if it clears what stops the assault.

fire missions enginedirect fire directcounterbattery out

terrain-and-special policy

An obstacle only counts if it's under fire

When Defending with engineers or a build option

  • Put obstacles only where a weapon covers them.
  • Keep them outside grenade range of own positions.
  • Use them to turn tanks into AT fire, not as a wall.
  • Guard any working party.

Uncovered mines delay only as long as it takes to bypass or lift them.

mine placement enginecoverage check proxyconstruction time out

terrain-and-special policy

In winter, shelter and roads decide

When Map is winter, with slow off-road movement

  • Value villages and woods more when choosing axes and held points.
  • Expect slow off-road flanks; plan shorter maneuvers.
  • Check tank routes before committing them.

Off-road movement slows, so held shelter and roads matter more.
